docs.title: 16.6 Designing memory at an advanced node: TSMC 7 nm and GlobalFoundries
docs.text:
What changes if you move from open 130 to 180 nm PDKs to a commercial advanced node such as TSMC N7? Much more becomes possible, but one thing stays the same: you still cannot make DRAM. N7 is a logic process with no DRAM capacitor technology.

A correction to a common belief

GlobalFoundries has no 7 nm process: it stopped 7 nm development in 2018. Its most advanced options are 12LP/12LP+ (FinFET) and 22FDX (FD-SOI).

Design Possible at N7? Industry relevance Notes SRAM macros (high-density, high-speed, low-voltage) Yes Very high TSMC-qualified bitcells; you design the periphery SRAM compiler Yes Very high What Arm, Synopsys and TSMC partners sell as IP Register files, TCAM, ROM Yes High In every CPU, GPU and network chip Compute-in-memory SRAM for AI Yes High Active research and startup area DDR5 / LPDDR5X controller and PHY Yes Very high N7/N6 are proven for LPDDR5/5X PHYs; LPDDR6 usually targets N3/N2 CXL memory expander controller Yes (needs a licensed PCIe/CXL PHY) High A real product category HBM base (logic) die Technically yes High Only useful with an HBM maker supplying the DRAM stack Gain-cell eDRAM (2T/3T) Yes (research) Medium DRAM-like, with refresh 1T1C DRAM No – No capacitor process at N7 Embedded MRAM / ReRAM Not at N7 – TSMC offers these at 40/28/22/16/12 nm NAND flash No – Needs a dedicated flash fab

GlobalFoundries options. GlobalFoundries is attractive for memory-rich designs that do not need the very latest density, particularly its FD-SOI process (fully depleted silicon-on-insulator: transistors on a thin silicon layer over a buried oxide, whose strength can be tuned after manufacture by a body-bias voltage applied underneath, which helps an SRAM run at a lower Vmin). 12LP/12LP+ (12 nm FinFET) suit SRAM, AI accelerators with large SRAM, controllers and PHYs. 22FDX/22FDX+ (22 nm FD-SOI) suit ultra-low-voltage SRAM and embedded MRAM for IoT, edge AI and automotive; it is the most memory-rich GF option. 14HP (14 nm FinFET with deep-trench) had real eDRAM, used for IBM POWER and Z caches, but is IBM-specific and not generally available.

How SRAM design changes at 7 nm. FinFET transistors come in whole fins, so widths are quantised and bitcells are named by their fin ratio: pull-up : pass-gate : pull-down fins, for example 111 (high density) or 122 (high current). Variation is so severe that assist circuits become mandatory, for example a negative-bitline write assist that briefly drives the bitline below ground to help flip the cell.

Aspect 130 nm open PDKs 7 nm FinFET Transistor sizing Any width Fin count only; bitcells named by fin ratio Bitcell You can design your own Use foundry pushed-rule bitcells; a custom cell needs deep foundry engagement Bitcell area ~2 µm² ~0.027 µm² high-density (~75× smaller) Variation Moderate Severe; high-sigma (6σ+) analysis needed Assist circuits Rarely needed Required: negative-bitline write assist, wordline underdrive, dual-rail supplies Layout Simple rules Multi-patterning colouring, restricted rules, thousands of DRC rules Reliability Mild Strict electromigration, self-heating and ageing limits Design focus Everything Periphery, assists, Vmin, power and the compiler

Example 16.3: Could you build 4 GB of SRAM at 7 nm?

A useful reference point is AMD's 3D V-Cache die: 64 MB of SRAM in about 41 mm² of TSMC 7 nm.

  1. \(4\ \text{GB} / 64\ \text{MB} = 4096/64 = 64\) V-Cache-sized blocks.
  2. Area: \(64 \times 41 = 2624\) mm², about 2600 mm².
  3. The reticle limit is about 858 mm², so \(2624/858 = 3.06\): about three maximum-size chips of pure SRAM.
  4. For another reference, the Cerebras WSE-2 (TSMC 7 nm) holds 40 GB of SRAM on an entire wafer.
  5. Cost per gigabyte is very roughly tens to over 100 times higher than DRAM.

So hundreds of megabytes of SRAM on a large die is feasible, and AI accelerators and big caches do exactly this, but bulk gigabytes still come from DRAM.

What you need to work at N7. An NDA with TSMC directly, or through a design-service partner or value chain aggregator (VCA) such as Global Unichip, Faraday or Alchip, or a university programme; the PDK, bitcells and SRAM compiler under NDA with secure IT; commercial, foundry-certified EDA (open-source tools do not support N7, and ASAP7 is predictive only); memory-specific tools such as Cadence Liberate MX, Synopsys PrimeLib and Solido; licensed IP (PLLs, I/O, PCIe/CXL PHYs, standard cells); silicon cost (an MPW slot roughly USD 100 to 500 thousand or more for a small test chip, a full mask set roughly USD 10 to 15 million or more); and a team (about 10 to 30 for an SRAM macro, 50 to 150 for a controller and PHY). A recommended order of projects is: (1) a low-Vmin, high-density SRAM macro and compiler using TSMC bitcells; (2) compute-in-memory SRAM for AI; (3) an LPDDR5X or DDR5 controller and PHY test chip; (4) a CXL memory expander controller; (5) gain-cell eDRAM. The suggested progression is to prove the methodology on open PDKs (SKY130, GF180MCU, IHP), then move to TSMC 16/12 nm or GF 22FDX through a university or design-service shuttle, then to N7 (or N5/N3).

docs.title: 16.7 Summary
docs.text:
• "Designing LPDDR6" means three jobs: the DRAM chip (only DRAM makers), the controller and PHY in an SoC (where most jobs are) and the package and board (with SI/PI tools).
  • LPDDR6 channels are 24 bits wide, with two 12-bit sub-channels, BL24 bursts of 256 data and 32 metadata bits, and up to 14.4 Gbps per pin.
  • The controller-and-PHY flow runs from reading the standard through RTL, UVM verification (50 to 70 per cent of the effort), analogue PHY and SI/PI to tapeout and lab bring-up; it takes 2.5 to 3.5 years, 100 to 150 people and USD 100 to 300 million, unless the IP is licensed.
  • DRAM design is full-custom analogue work needing fast-SPICE and high-sigma tools; the real barrier is the fab (USD 15 to 20 billion), not the tools.
  • At TSMC N7 one can design SRAM, controllers, PHYs and compute-in-memory, but not DRAM; GlobalFoundries has no 7 nm process.

docs.title: 16.8 Exercises
docs.text:
Exercise 16.1. How many bits does a 12-bit LPDDR6 sub-channel carry in one burst of 24, and what fraction are metadata?

Answer

\(24 \times 12 = 288\) bits; 256 are data and 32 are metadata, a fraction of \(32/288 = 11.1\) per cent.

Exercise 16.2. An LPDDR6 channel has two 12-bit sub-channels at 14.4 Gbps. Find its raw bandwidth and compare it with an LPDDR5X channel at 10.7 Gbps.

Answer

LPDDR6: \(24 \times 14.4 / 8 = 43.2\) GB/s. LPDDR5X: \(16 \times 10.7 / 8 = 21.4\) GB/s. The LPDDR6 channel offers about 2.0 times as much raw bandwidth.

Exercise 16.3. Why is a verification engineer team usually the largest group in a controller-and-PHY project?

Answer

Verification takes 50 to 70 per cent of the effort: testbenches (UVM), verification IP, timing checkers, formal proofs and long emulation runs must prove the design against the whole standard before an expensive tapeout. Design verification has 20 to 40 people, the largest group in the team table.

Exercise 16.4. Name the open-source tool that substitutes for each commercial tool in learning: Virtuoso, Spectre, Calibre, StarRC, JasperGold, PrimeTime.

Answer

Virtuoso: Xschem with Magic or KLayout. Spectre: ngspice (or Xyce). Calibre: KLayout DRC/LVS and Netgen. StarRC: Magic or OpenRCX. JasperGold: SymbiYosys. PrimeTime: OpenSTA.

Exercise 16.5. An 8 GB SRAM block at 7 nm would need how many V-Cache-sized (64 MB, 41 mm²) blocks and how much area? How many reticle-sized chips?

Answer

\(8\ \text{GB}/64\ \text{MB} = 128\) blocks, so \(128 \times 41 = 5248\) mm². With an 858 mm² reticle limit, \(5248/858 = 6.1\): about six or seven maximum-size chips.

Exercise 16.6 (Project: a controller study). Choose one of the following for a small project: (a) compare two request-scheduling policies with Ramulator 2.0 or DRAMSim3; (b) read the LiteDRAM sources and list the blocks of its controller; (c) write a simplified LPDDR-style controller in SystemVerilog, test it with Verilator and cocotb. State what you will deliver.

Answer

There is no single answer; a good scope delivers working, measured results. For (a), run the same traffic with, say, first-come-first-served and a policy that prefers already-open rows, and report the row-hit rate and bandwidth. For (b), a list that includes command queues, a scheduler, a refresh manager and the PHY interface. For (c), a controller with an activate, read, precharge sequence and refresh, and a cocotb model that flags every timing violation (as in Exercise 3.5).

docs.title: Chapter 15: Designing an SRAM, Process Kits and Process Nodes
docs.text: The earlier chapters treated chips as products. This chapter looks at how a memory chip is designed and made, using the one memory that a student team can realistically take all the way to silicon: a small SRAM block. It walks through the design flow step by step, from specification to tapeout, shows the shortcut offered by the OpenRAM compiler, lists the files handed to the fabricator, and then explains the two ideas that decide what is possible: the process design kit (the factory's rule book) and the process node (and why a DRAM "12 nm" is not a logic "7 nm"). It ends with the trend that makes SRAM a growing problem for processor designers: its cell has almost stopped shrinking.

docs.title: 15.1 Why SRAM, and not DRAM?
docs.text: A 6T SRAM cell is made only of ordinary transistors, so it can be built on any standard CMOS logic process, including the open, academic processes such as SKY130, GF180MCU and IHP SG13G2 that students can actually fabricate on. A DRAM 1T1C cell is different: it needs a capacitor that is very tall and thin (built as a deep trench or a stacked cylinder) and a special low-leakage access transistor. These need a dedicated DRAM process that only memory fabs such as Samsung, SK hynix and Micron run. As a result, designing a DRAM from scratch is not possible on normal or academic shuttle runs, while designing an SRAM is a realistic and very instructive project.

docs.title: 15.2 The design flow, step by step
docs.text:
Designing a chip is like building a house with a very strict inspector. The stages are: specification (how big, how fast, how much power: "a three-bedroom house"), architecture (banks, decoders, sense amplifiers, I/O: the floor plan), circuit design (transistor schematics simulated in SPICE: wiring each room), layout (the exact shapes on each layer, in nanometres: the blueprint), verification with DRC and LVS (rule checks and "layout equals schematic": the inspector), tapeout (sending the GDSII file to the factory), fabrication (about three months and hundreds of process steps) and packaging and test (every chip is tested, and bad bits are repaired with spare rows).

Why so much checking?

A mistake found in simulation costs minutes. Found after fabrication, it costs a new set of masks (millions of dollars at advanced nodes) and months. So designers simulate every corner: hot, cold, fast silicon, slow silicon, high and low voltage.

The sections below take the stages for a small SRAM macro (a hard block that is placed in a larger chip) in eleven steps.

Step 1: Specification. Write down what the memory must do before drawing anything: the capacity and organisation (for example 1K × 32: 1024 words of 32 bits, 32 Kbit in total); the number and type of ports (single-port, true dual-port, or one read plus one write port, 1R1W); the target clock frequency and access time; the power budget (energy per access and standby leakage); the supply voltage; and the process with its PDK, for example SKY130, GF180MCU, IHP SG13G2 or a commercial TSMC 65 nm process. Every later decision is checked against this specification.

Step 2: Architecture. Decide how the bits are arranged. A 1K × 32 memory could be 1024 rows of 32 cells, but such a tall, thin array has very long bitlines (slow) and a large decoder. Designers usually fold it: with a 4:1 column multiplexer it becomes 256 rows × 128 columns, and each output bit chooses one of four neighbouring columns (8:1 is also common). Large memories are split into banks to keep wordlines and bitlines short. Timing can come directly from the clock (simple, but every step must allow for the worst case) or from a self-timed replica bitline: a dummy column built to discharge like the slowest real column, which fires the sense amplifiers at just the right moment and automatically tracks process, voltage and temperature.

Figure 15.1. Main blocks of an SRAM macro: row decoder and wordline drivers, bitcell array of 256 rows by 128 columns, precharge and equalisation, column mux, sense amplifiers, write drivers, data latches, a replica bitline and a control and timing block that generates the sense-amplifier enable

Example 15.1: Folding a 1K × 32 SRAM

  1. Capacity: \(1024 \times 32 = 32{,}768\) bits \(= 32\) Kbit. The address has \(\log_2 1024 = 10\) bits.
  2. Folding with a 4:1 column multiplexer: the array has \(1024/4 = 256\) rows and \(32 \times 4 = 128\) columns, and \(256 \times 128 = 32{,}768\) cells as required.
  3. The row decoder takes 8 address bits (\(2^8 = 256\) rows); the column multiplexer takes the other 2 bits to choose one of four neighbouring columns for each of the 32 output bits.
  4. Area estimate on SKY130, using the numbers of Chapter 17: a 6T cell is about 2 µm², and the area per bit including periphery is about 3.3 µm² (about 60 per cent array efficiency). So the block is about \(32{,}768 \times 3.3 = 108{,}000\) µm², or about 0.11 mm².

Step 3: Bitcell design. The 6T cell must be read-stable (a read must not flip it) and writable (a write must flip it). Read stability depends on the cell ratio, which must be comfortably greater than one; writability depends on the pull-up ratio (Section 2.2). Designers measure the static noise margin (SNM) in hold and read, and the write margin, often from butterfly curves. Because transistors vary randomly and a memory holds millions of cells, Monte Carlo simulation over many random samples checks that the margins hold far out into the statistical tail. If the foundry offers a pushed-rule bitcell, a cell drawn with special tighter rules that the foundry has qualified, use it: it is much smaller than anything that can be drawn with normal rules.

Step 4: Peripheral circuits. Design the circuits around the array: a predecoder and decoder that turn the row address into one active row; wordline drivers strong enough to switch a long, heavily loaded wordline quickly; bitline precharge and equalisation transistors that set both bitlines to the same voltage before each access; a latch-type sense amplifier that resolves a small bitline difference into a full logic level when sense-enable fires; write drivers that pull one bitline low; the column multiplexer; and the control logic with its replica timing path.

Step 5: SPICE simulation. Simulate the critical path (address input, decoder, wordline, bitline discharge, sense amplifier and output) with a SPICE circuit simulator: ngspice or Xyce (open source), HSPICE or Spectre (commercial). Check read, write and hold at every PVT corner (process, voltage, temperature): process corners TT, FF, SS, FS and SF (typical, fast or slow NMOS and PMOS), supply ±10 per cent, and temperature from −40 to 125 °C. Measure access time, minimum cycle time, energy per read and write, and leakage. Run Monte Carlo on the sense amplifier: its input offset must be safely smaller than the bitline difference that has developed when sense-enable fires.

Step 6: Layout. Draw the physical shapes in a layout editor: Magic or KLayout (open source) or Cadence Virtuoso (commercial). Start with the leaf cells (bitcell, sense amplifier, drivers) and tile them. The periphery must be pitch-matched: each sense amplifier or wordline driver must fit exactly into the width or height of one or a few bitcells so that the blocks line up. Add a power grid, well taps (which tie the wells to the supply and prevent latch-up), guard rings around sensitive circuits, and dummy rows and columns at the array edge so that the outermost real cells see the same surroundings as the inner ones.

Step 7: Physical verification. DRC (design rule check) confirms that every shape obeys the foundry's width, spacing and enclosure rules; the result must be clean or covered by foundry-approved waivers. LVS (layout versus schematic) extracts a circuit from the layout and proves that it matches the schematic. Antenna, ERC (electrical rule check) and density checks complete the set. Tools: Magic, KLayout and Netgen (open source); Siemens Calibre or Cadence Pegasus (commercial).

Step 8: Parasitic extraction and post-layout simulation. Real wires have resistance and capacitance. PEX (parasitic extraction) adds them to the netlist; long bitlines and wordlines in particular become slower. Re-simulate the critical paths with parasitics, then fix and iterate: resize drivers, adjust the replica timing or change the floorplan.

Step 9: Characterisation and views. Digital tools cannot simulate the whole SRAM at transistor level, so abstract views are generated: a Liberty .lib file with timing and power tables for each corner, a LEF abstract (outline, pin positions and blocked metal) for place-and-route tools, and a Verilog behavioural model for logic simulation.

Step 10: Chip integration. Place the macro in a full chip: a pad ring with ESD (electrostatic discharge) protection on every pin, power and ground pads, a seal ring around the die edge, and usually a BIST (built-in self-test) engine that writes and reads test patterns. Then run full-chip DRC and LVS, add metal and polysilicon fill to meet density rules, and complete the signoff checklist.

Step 11: Tapeout. Send the final layout to the foundry, or to a multi-project wafer (MPW) shuttle in which many designs share one mask set and wafer run to split the cost. Academic routes include Europractice, MOSIS and IHP's own shuttles. Chips typically come back some months later for packaging and lab testing.

docs.title: 15.3 The shortcut: OpenRAM
docs.text:
OpenRAM is an open-source SRAM compiler that automates steps 2 to 9. You give it the word size, the number of words and the number of ports, and it generates the netlist, layout, .lib, .lef and Verilog model and runs DRC and LVS. It supports SKY130, GF180MCU and the predictive FreePDK45, among others. A good learning plan is to generate a memory with OpenRAM first, then study, simulate and modify the circuits it produced.

A student route through the open tools has five steps: simulate a 6T cell (Xschem and ngspice); generate an SRAM (the OpenRAM compiler); check the layout (Magic or KLayout, with Netgen); build the chip (LibreLane, the successor of OpenLane); and tape out to a shuttle, then test the silicon.

Stage Open-source option Process design kit (PDK) SKY130, GF180MCU, IHP SG13G2 Schematic capture Xschem Circuit simulation ngspice, Xyce Layout Magic, KLayout DRC / LVS Magic, KLayout, Netgen SRAM compiler OpenRAM Full chip (RTL to GDS) OpenLane / LibreLane

docs.title: 15.4 Files given to the fabricator
docs.text:
At tapeout the foundry or shuttle operator needs a small, well-defined set of files. The layout file is the real product; the rest proves that it is correct and tells the fab how to handle it.

File Purpose Required? GDSII (.gds) or OASIS (.oas) Final layout with all mask layers; the main deliverable Mandatory Layer map / mask layer list Maps GDS layer numbers to foundry mask layers Usually DRC report (clean) and waiver list Proves compliance with the design rules Usually LVS report Shows the layout matches the netlist Often requested Tapeout form / checklist Die size, top-cell name, process options, metal stack, number of dies, shuttle ID Mandatory Density / fill report Metal and poly density rules met (some foundries add fill themselves) Usually Seal ring and scribe information Die boundary for dicing Usually built into the GDS Bonding diagram / pad list For the packaging house If packaging is ordered Netlist (CDL/SPICE) Some foundries run their own LVS Sometimes

Kept in-house, not sent to the fab: schematics; SPICE netlists and simulation results; the .lib, .lef and Verilog models; and the test plan and test vectors used when the chips come back.

docs.title: 15.5 The factory's rule book: the PDK
docs.text:
A PDK (process design kit) is the rulebook and the set of models for one fab's process: it tells designers and tools what can be drawn and how the resulting devices will behave. Commercial PDKs (TSMC, Samsung) are secret and need an agreement. The open PDKs SkyWater SKY130, GlobalFoundries GF180 and IHP SG13G2 are free on GitHub. Because a PDK is derived from measurements of real wafers, you cannot create a PDK for TSMC or Samsung without their process data.

Component What it is Formats / tools Device models SPICE models with corners and Monte Carlo statistics BSIM4, BSIM-CMG, BSIM-BULK; .lib / .scs files Design rule manual Human-readable rules: widths, spacings, enclosures PDF DRC deck Machine-readable design rules Calibre SVRF, KLayout DRC, Magic techfile LVS deck Device recognition and netlist comparison Calibre, Netgen, KLayout LVS PEX deck Parasitic extraction rules StarRC ITF / nxtgrd, Quantus ICT / qrcTechFile, Magic extraction Techfile and layer map Layer definitions and display Virtuoso techfile, KLayout .lyp / .lyt, LEF technology PCells Parameterised device layouts SKILL, PyCell, KLayout Python, gdsfactory Symbols Schematic symbols for each device Virtuoso, Xschem Standard-cell library Logic gates for digital design GDS, LEF, Liberty .lib, Verilog I/O and ESD library Pads and protection GDS, LEF, .lib Reliability rules Electromigration limits, ageing, ESD Documents and decks DFM rules Fill and lithography-hotspot rules Decks Memory compilers (optional) Generate SRAM blocks Compiler software

How a PDK is built. There are nine steps. (1) Define the process: choose the masks, layer thicknesses, doping and gate oxide, and draft the first design rules from what the lithography and etch tools can reliably achieve. (2) Simulate with TCAD (technology computer-aided design), which gives first estimates of device behaviour before any silicon exists. (3) Design test chips: transistors of many widths and lengths, resistors, capacitors, diodes, ring oscillators, contact and via chains, yield structures, and structures that test each design rule. (4) Measure wafers with a probe station and parameter analyser (I–V and C–V curves, sheet resistance and leakage across many wafers and lots). (5) Extract models by fitting BSIM parameters to the measurements and creating corner and statistical models. (6) Write the DRC, LVS and PEX decks. (7) Build the design libraries: PCells, symbols and standard cells, characterised for timing and power. (8) Qualify and correlate with a test design (ring oscillators, an SRAM, a small CPU) and check that silicon matches simulation. (9) Release, document, version and maintain.

Kind of PDK Team Time Academic or older process (1 µm–180 nm) 2–10 people 1–2 years Predictive / educational (ASAP7, FreePDK) 3–10 researchers 1–2 years Commercial advanced node 100–300+ engineers Years, with continuous updates PDK Type Node Manufacturable? SKY130 (SkyWater) Real, open 130 nm Yes GF180MCU (GlobalFoundries) Real, open 180 nm Yes IHP SG13G2 Real, open, SiGe BiCMOS 130 nm Yes, via IHP shuttles ASAP7 (ASU and Arm) Predictive 7 nm FinFET No FreePDK45 / FreePDK15 (NC State) Predictive 45 / 15 nm No PTM models (ASU) Predictive models only 130 nm down to 7 nm No LibreSilicon Community, experimental ~1 µm Experimental

What does this mean for RAM projects? No public DRAM PDK exists, so DRAM cell design can only be studied, not fabricated, outside the memory companies. SRAM is fully possible on SKY130, GF180MCU and IHP SG13G2, and OpenRAM supports SKY130 and GF180MCU. ASAP7 lets you simulate a 7 nm FinFET SRAM cell and see modern scaling effects. Building a small PDK for a college or institute nanofab (for example a 1 to 2 µm CMOS process) makes an excellent final-year or research project.

docs.title: 15.6 What "nm" means for memory
docs.text:
Logic chips are sold as "7 nm", "3 nm" or "2 nm". DRAM uses a completely different naming system, and the numbers cannot be compared directly.

DRAM node names. Since about 2016 DRAM makers have named their processes as generations of a "10 nm class": 1x, 1y, 1z, then the Greek letters 1α, 1β, 1γ. The number loosely tracks the half-pitch of the memory array, half the distance between repeated lines such as wordlines, which is a real physical dimension. EUV (extreme ultraviolet) lithography, which prints the finest patterns in one exposure, entered DRAM production at 1z/1α.

Node Approx. half-pitch Mass production EUV used? 1x ~18–19 nm ~2016 No 1y ~17 nm ~2018 No 1z ~15–16 nm ~2019–20 Samsung: 1 layer 1α (1a) ~14 nm ~2021 Samsung and SK hynix yes; Micron no 1β (1b) ~12–13 nm ~2022–23 Samsung and SK hynix yes; Micron no 1γ (1c) ~11–12 nm ~2024–25 Yes (Micron's first EUV node) 1δ / 0a ~10 nm and below ~2026–27+ Yes, more layers 3D DRAM / 4F² vertical-channel cells Below 10 nm equivalent ~2028–2030+ In research and development

Feature sizes are approximate: vendors do not publish exact dimensions. Micron uses Greek letters (1α, 1β, 1γ), while Samsung and SK hynix use 1a, 1b, 1c; Samsung also markets its 1b node as "12 nm-class". 4F² refers to a cell area of four times the square of the feature size, smaller than today's 6F² cells.

Why DRAM "12 nm" is not logic "7 nm".

Aspect DRAM "12 nm-class" Logic "7 nm" (e.g. TSMC N7) What the number means Roughly a real half-pitch of the memory array A marketing name; actual gate pitch is about 57 nm and tightest metal pitch about 40 nm Optimised for Density, ultra-low leakage, very tall capacitors Transistor speed and drive current Array transistor Buried-channel array transistor (buried wordline) FinFET, now gate-all-around (GAA) nanosheets Hardest structure Storage capacitor with aspect ratio above 50:1 Transistor and dense metal wiring

A DRAM cell must hold a tiny charge for around 64 ms between refreshes, so its access transistor must leak almost nothing and its capacitor must be as large as possible in a tiny footprint. That leads to capacitors more than fifty times taller than they are wide, and to buried wordline transistors (BCAT) whose gate sits in a trench below the silicon surface to give a long effective channel. Logic processes make the opposite trade: fast, leaky transistors and many layers of wiring. This is why DRAM and logic are made in different fabs, and why their "nm" numbers measure different things.

Which node each RAM type uses (2025 to 2026).

RAM type Typical process node DDR4 1x / 1y / 1z DDR5 1α, 1β, now 1γ / 1c LPDDR5X 1β, 1γ / 1c LPDDR6 1γ / 1c GDDR6 1y–1α GDDR7 1β (some 1γ) HBM3E (DRAM dies) 1β HBM4 (DRAM dies) 1β / 1c HBM4 (base die) A logic process (for example TSMC 12 nm, 5 nm or 3 nm, or Samsung 4 nm), the first time HBM uses a logic node for its base die On-chip SRAM Same node as the processor (5 nm, 3 nm, 2 nm, Intel 18A) Standalone SRAM 28–90 nm PSRAM ~25–65 nm RLDRAM Older DRAM nodes Embedded MRAM 28 / 22 / 16 / 12 nm, moving to 14 / 8 nm Standalone MRAM 28–40 nm FeRAM ~130 nm ReRAM (embedded) 40 / 28 / 22 nm LPDDR6 controller + PHY (inside the SoC) 3 nm / 2 nm

SRAM scaling has stalled. For decades each new logic node shrank the SRAM bitcell substantially. That has slowed sharply: the high-density 6T cell barely shrank from TSMC N5 to N3E, and gate-all-around transistors at N2 brought only a modest gain (Figure 15.2, approximate published figures). Because caches are a large share of a modern processor's area, this is a serious problem. One response is to build SRAM on a separate, cheaper die and stack it on the processor, as AMD does with 3D V-Cache.

Figure 15.2. Approximate high-density 6T SRAM bitcell area in square micrometres: TSMC N7 about 0.027 (FinFET), N5 about 0.021 (FinFET), N3E about 0.021 (FinFET, no shrink against N5), N2 about 0.0175 (GAA nanosheet)

Example 15.2: How much did the SRAM cell really shrink?

  1. N7 to N5: \(0.027 \to 0.021\) µm², an area ratio of \(0.021/0.027 = 0.78\), a 22 per cent reduction.
  2. N5 to N3E: \(0.021 \to 0.021\), ratio 1.0: no shrink at all.
  3. N3E to N2: \(0.021 \to 0.0175\), ratio 0.83, a 17 per cent reduction.
  4. N7 to N2 overall: \(0.0175/0.027 = 0.65\), so the cell is 35 per cent smaller after three node steps, about 1.5 times denser.
  5. For comparison, the SKY130 6T cell of about 2 µm² is \(2/0.027 = 74\) times larger than the N7 cell, and a DRAM cell of about 0.001 µm² is 27 times smaller than the N7 SRAM cell.

docs.title: 15.7 Summary
docs.text:
• SRAM is the only memory a student team can take to silicon: it needs only ordinary logic transistors, while DRAM needs a dedicated process with very tall capacitors that only memory fabs run.
  • The SRAM flow has eleven steps: specification, architecture, bitcell, periphery, SPICE simulation, layout, physical verification, extraction, characterisation, integration and tapeout. OpenRAM automates steps 2 to 9.
  • The PDK holds device models, design rules, rule decks and cell libraries; the open PDKs are SKY130 (130 nm), GF180MCU (180 nm) and IHP SG13G2 (130 nm SiGe BiCMOS).
  • DRAM node names (1α, 1β, 1γ) track a real half-pitch of the array; logic "nm" names are marketing. DRAM and logic differ in what they optimise (leakage and tall capacitors against speed).
  • The 6T SRAM cell has almost stopped shrinking: no shrink from N5 to N3E, 17 per cent from N3E to N2.

docs.title: 15.8 Exercises
docs.text:
Exercise 15.1. A 2K × 16 SRAM is folded with an 8:1 column multiplexer. How many address bits, rows and columns does it have, and how many bits go to the row decoder?

Answer

Words: 2048, so 11 address bits. Array: rows \(= 2048/8 = 256\), columns \(= 16 \times 8 = 128\) (\(256 \times 128 = 32{,}768\) cells, 32 Kbit). Row decoder: 8 bits; the column multiplexer takes the other 3 bits.

Exercise 15.2. Using 3.3 µm² per bit on SKY130, estimate the area of a 4 KB (32 Kbit) SRAM macro, and how many such macros fit into a 10 mm² shuttle slot?

Answer

\(4\ \text{KB} = 32{,}768\) bits. Area \(= 32{,}768 \times 3.3 = 108{,}000\) µm² \(= 0.108\) mm². In 10 mm²: \(10/0.108 \approx 92\) macros, ignoring pad ring, routing and test logic.

Exercise 15.3. Why does the SRAM flow use a replica bitline for timing?

Answer

The replica bitline is a dummy column that discharges like the slowest real column, so it fires the sense amplifiers at just the right moment. Because it is built from the same devices, it tracks process, voltage and temperature automatically, without allowing a fixed worst-case delay at every step.

Exercise 15.4. Match each file to the stage that needs it: (a) Gerber files; (b) GDSII; (c) ATE test program; (d) bonding diagram. Stages: PCB fab, DRAM fab, OSAT, tester.

Answer

(a) PCB fab and assembly. (b) The DRAM fab (silicon). (c) The tester. (d) The OSAT (packaging).

Exercise 15.5. A student wants to design a 4 Gb DRAM chip on a SKY130 shuttle. Explain why this cannot work, using the cell and the process.

Answer

A DRAM 1T1C cell needs a very tall, thin capacitor (aspect ratio above 50:1) and a low-leakage access transistor. The open processes have no deep-capacitor or buried-wordline technology; only memory fabs have such a process, and no open DRAM PDK exists. The metal-insulator-metal capacitors available on open PDKs are far too large. Even with SRAM in place of DRAM, 4 Gb would need about 115,000 mm² at SKY130, about 130 times the largest chip a factory can print (Chapter 17).

Exercise 15.6 (Assignment 13: generate and inspect a real SRAM). Configure OpenRAM for 256 words × 32 bits on SKY130. Open the GDS in KLayout and find the bitcell array, the decoders and the sense amplifiers. Run DRC (Magic) and LVS (Netgen) and read the .lib timing file.

Answer

A configuration file is as short as word_size = 32, num_words = 256, tech_name = "sky130", run with python3 sram_compiler.py myconfig.py from the OpenRAM checkout (start from an example configuration shipped with OpenRAM and change only the size). Success means the GDS opens, LVS reports a match, and you can name each region of the layout. Deliver screenshots of each block, the DRC and LVS results and the macro area. The block is 1 KB, in the range of 1 KB to a few hundred KB that suits a test chip.

docs.title: Glossary
docs.text: AOI Automated optical inspection: camera-based checking of assembled boards for defects. Array efficiency The fraction of a memory die's area occupied by storage cells rather than periphery and wiring. ATE Automatic test equipment: production testers that apply patterns to chips and measure the results (for example Advantest, Teradyne). Bank An independent memory array inside a DRAM chip with its own row buffer; different banks can work in parallel. Bank group A set of banks sharing some internal circuits; switching between bank groups is faster than staying in one (DDR4 and later). BCAT / buried wordline A DRAM access transistor whose gate (the wordline) is buried in a trench below the silicon surface, giving a long effective channel and very low leakage in a tiny area (BCAT: buried-channel array transistor). Bit, byte One 0-or-1 value; eight bits make a byte. Bitline, wordline The column wire that carries the data of the cells, and the row wire that opens them. BOM Bill of materials: the list of every component to buy. BSIM Berkeley short-channel IGFET model: the industry-standard family of SPICE transistor models (BSIM4, BSIM-CMG for FinFETs, BSIM-BULK). Burn-in Running parts at elevated temperature and voltage to make weak units fail before shipment. Burst length (BL) The number of consecutive transfers per read or write command, for example BL16 in DDR5. CAS latency (CL) The clock cycles from a column read command to the first data; convert to nanoseconds with CL × 2000 ÷ MT/s. Channel An independent path between memory controller and memory, with its own command and data wires. Courtyard The keep-out area around a part on a board that other parts may not enter. CRC Cyclic redundancy check: a checksum that detects corrupted data. CXL Compute Express Link: a cache-coherent protocol over PCIe wiring, used to attach memory expanders and pooled memory. CXL memory expander A device that adds DRAM capacity to a server through a CXL link instead of DIMM slots. Datasheet The manufacturer's full specification of a part: pins, voltages, timings, currents. Decoupling capacitor A small local energy tank that steadies the supply voltage. DFI DDR PHY Interface: the standard interface between a memory controller and the PHY on a chip. DIMM Dual in-line memory module: a circuit board of DRAM chips that plugs into a slot. An RDIMM is registered, with an RCD chip buffering the commands. DRAM Dynamic RAM: one transistor and one capacitor per bit; must be refreshed. DRC Design rule check: verifies that every layout shape obeys the foundry's geometric rules. DVFS Dynamic voltage and frequency scaling: lowering voltage and clock when full speed is not needed, to save power. ECC Error-correcting code: extra bits that let errors be detected and corrected (side-band, on-die or inline). eMRAM Embedded MRAM: magnetic memory built into a logic chip as non-volatile code or data storage. EMS Electronics manufacturing services: companies that assemble and test boards for other firms. EUV Extreme ultraviolet lithography (13.5 nm wavelength), used to print the finest layers of advanced logic and DRAM. Eye diagram Many bits overlaid; the open gap shows the voltage and timing margin. Fast-SPICE Circuit simulators that trade a little accuracy for huge speed-ups, making it possible to simulate whole memory arrays with parasitics. FD-SOI / body bias Fully depleted silicon-on-insulator: transistors on a thin silicon layer over a buried oxide. A body-bias voltage beneath tunes transistor strength, for example to lower SRAM Vmin. FinFET fin ratio FinFET bitcells are named by fin counts of pull-up : pass-gate : pull-down transistors, for example 111 (high density) or 122 (high current). Fly-by One wire visiting several chips in a row, like bus stops; write levelling compensates for the arrival delays. Gain-cell eDRAM Embedded DRAM using two or three ordinary transistors, storing charge on a transistor gate instead of a dedicated capacitor; needs refresh. GDSII The standard binary file format for chip layouts (layers of polygons), sent to the foundry at tapeout. Gerber The file format of each PCB layer sent to the board factory. Half-pitch Half the repeat distance of a regular pattern such as DRAM wordlines; used to name DRAM process nodes. High-sigma analysis Statistical methods that show a circuit still works at very rare variation levels (for example 6 sigma) without running billions of Monte Carlo samples. IDM Integrated device manufacturer: a company that both designs and manufactures its chips (for example Samsung, Micron, Intel). Impedance (Z0) How a wire resists a fast signal; set by trace width and spacing to the plane. Interposer A silicon (or organic) layer with fine wiring that connects dies placed side by side, for example a GPU and HBM stacks. ISM / DLI scheme The India Semiconductor Mission and its Design Linked Incentive scheme, which supports chip design and tapeout costs for Indian companies. JEDEC The industry standards body that publishes the DDR, LPDDR, GDDR and HBM specifications. LVS Layout versus schematic: proves that the circuit drawn in the layout matches the schematic netlist. MBIST / March C− Memory built-in self-test: on-chip logic that tests a memory. March C− is a classic test sequence of ordered writes and reads that detects common cell faults. Mirroring (MIR) Swapping pin functions so that chips on the back side of a board can be wired straight through. MPW / shuttle Multi-project wafer: many designs share one mask set and wafer run to split the cost. Organised shuttle programmes (for example Europractice and MOSIS) sell slots on scheduled runs. MT/s Megatransfers per second: how many times per second each data pin carries a new symbol. Net One electrical connection: every pin that must be joined together. NRZ Non-return-to-zero: two-level signalling, one bit per symbol. OASIS A newer, more compact layout file format than GDSII, used for very large designs. OPC Optical proximity correction: deliberate distortion of mask shapes so that the printed pattern on the wafer matches the intended layout. OSAT Outsourced semiconductor assembly and test company (for example ASE, Amkor, JCET). PAM3, PAM4 Pulse amplitude modulation with 3 or 4 voltage levels, carrying 1.5 or 2 bits per symbol. PDK Process design kit: a foundry's device models, design rules, rule decks and libraries for one process. PDN Power delivery network: everything between the regulator and the chip. PEX Parasitic extraction: computes wire resistance and capacitance from layout for post-layout simulation. PHY The physical-layer circuits that drive and receive signals on the pins (drivers, receivers, clocking, training). Plane A whole layer of copper used for ground or one supply voltage. PMIC Power-management IC; on DDR5 modules it converts the supply into the voltages the DRAM needs. PoP Package-on-package: memory stacked directly on top of the processor package, common in phones. Prefetch The number of bits per data pin fetched from the array in one internal access (2n, 4n, 8n, 16n). PVT Process, voltage and temperature: the corners across which a circuit must work. QVL Qualified vendor list: memory parts that a platform or server maker has tested and approved. RAM Random-access memory: fast working memory in which any location is reached in about the same time; it forgets when the power is off. Rank A set of DRAM chips that together fill the channel width and are accessed together. "1Rx4" means one rank built from x4 chips. Raw card A JEDEC reference PCB design for a given memory module type and DRAM organisation. RCD Registering clock driver: buffers command, address and clock signals on RDIMMs, LRDIMMs and MRDIMMs, so the controller sees one load per module. Reflection coefficient (Γ) The fraction of a signal that bounces back from a mismatched end: \((R - Z_0)/(R + Z_0)\). Refresh Periodically reading and rewriting DRAM rows so that leaking capacitors do not lose their data. Reticle limit The largest area a lithography scanner can expose in one shot, about 26 × 33 mm (about 858 mm²); the maximum size of one chip. Rowhammer / PRAC Rowhammer: repeatedly activating a row can flip bits in neighbouring rows. PRAC (per-row activation counting) tracks activations so the DRAM can trigger protective refresh. Sense amplifier A circuit that detects a tiny voltage difference and turns it into a clean 0 or 1. Shmoo plot A pass/fail map of a chip measured across two variables, typically supply voltage and frequency. SI / PI Signal integrity and power integrity: analysis of signal quality on wires and of the power delivery network. SPD hub The DDR5 module chip holding the SPD data (and often a temperature sensor), read by the BIOS over I²C or I3C. SPICE The family of circuit simulators; ngspice is the open-source one. SRAM Static RAM: six transistors per bit; fast, no refresh; used for caches. Stack-up The order and thickness of copper and insulation layers in a PCB. Static noise margin (SNM) How much noise a stored SRAM bit can tolerate before it flips, measured from butterfly curves. Tapeout Sending a finished chip design to be manufactured. TCAD Technology computer-aided design: physics-based simulation of process steps and devices. Termination / ODT A resistor (often inside the chip, as on-die termination) that absorbs a signal to stop echoes. TSV Through-silicon via: a vertical connection through a thinned die, used to stack HBM dies. UVM Universal Verification Methodology: a standard SystemVerilog framework for building reusable testbenches. VCA Value chain aggregator: a design-service company authorised to give smaller customers access to a foundry (for example Global Unichip, Faraday, Alchip). Via A plated hole that connects copper on different layers. VIP Verification IP: ready-made models and protocol checkers for a standard interface such as LPDDR6 or AXI. Vmin The lowest supply voltage at which a memory still reads and writes correctly. Vref Reference voltage that a receiver compares an incoming signal against to decide whether it is a 0 or a 1. Write assist / negative bitline Circuits that help an SRAM write succeed at low voltage; a negative-bitline assist briefly drives the bitline below ground. Write levelling Calibration that compensates for the different arrival times of a fly-by command bus.

docs.title: Chapter 7: HBM and Specialty DRAM
docs.text: High Bandwidth Memory stacks DRAM dies vertically and connects them to the processor through a very wide, short interface. It delivers by far the most bandwidth of any memory and is the defining memory of the AI era. This chapter explains how a stack is built, why accelerators need it, what it costs, and how its generations compare. The second half turns to the specialty and historic DRAMs, the designs adapted for special jobs, some of which are still made while others matter mainly as history that shaped modern designs.

docs.title: 7.1 How HBM is built
docs.text:
An HBM stack is a tower of DRAM dies, 8, 12 or 16 high in current parts, sitting on a base die, also called the logic die. Each DRAM die is thinned and pierced by thousands of TSVs (through-silicon vias): vertical copper connections that carry signals and power straight through the silicon. The base die contains the interface circuits (the PHY), test logic and buffers.

Instead of a few fast pins, HBM uses a very wide, relatively slow bus: 1024 bits per stack up to HBM3E, and 2048 bits for HBM4. So many wires cannot run through an ordinary circuit board, so the stacks and the processor sit side by side on a silicon interposer, a slab of silicon with very fine wiring. This is called 2.5D packaging, and TSMC's CoWoS (chip-on-wafer-on-substrate) is the best-known example. Because the wires are only millimetres long, each bit costs little energy to move.

Figure 7.1. Cross-section of a GPU or system chip with two HBM stacks on a silicon interposer over a package substrate with solder balls, labelling DRAM core dies, TSVs, the base logic die, the interposer, the substrate and the solder balls

Figure 7.1 is a simplified cross-section, not to scale; real accelerators carry up to eight or more stacks.

docs.title: 7.2 Why AI needs HBM
docs.text:
Training and running large AI models is often limited not by arithmetic but by how fast model weights and activations can be streamed from memory. When generating text, for example, every new token may require reading most of the model's weights. An accelerator with eight HBM3E stacks has roughly 8 TB/s of bandwidth. Capacity matters too: bigger stacks let larger models fit on fewer chips.

Example 7.1: HBM bandwidth against a desktop

  1. One HBM3E stack at 9.6 Gbps per pin: \(9.6 \times 1024 / 8 = 1228.8\) GB/s, about 1.2 TB/s.
  2. Eight such stacks: \(8 \times 1.2288 = 9.8\) TB/s. At the lower end of the HBM3E speed range (9.2 Gbps) eight stacks give \(8 \times 1177.6 = 9.4\) TB/s; the figure "8 to 10 TB/s" covers the range of accelerators.
  3. A dual-channel DDR5-6400 desktop reaches 102.4 GB/s (Example 1.2). The ratio is \(9830 / 102.4 \approx 96\) for ten TB/s, and \(8000/102.4 \approx 78\) for 8 TB/s.

So an eight-stack accelerator has roughly 80 to 95 times the bandwidth of a dual-channel desktop.

A correction

The tutorial text says "more than a hundred times a dual-channel desktop" for 8 TB/s. The arithmetic gives 78 to 96 times, so "roughly eighty to ninety times" is the accurate statement.

docs.title: 7.3 Cost and supply
docs.text: HBM is expensive: it costs several times more per gigabyte than DDR5, because stacking, TSVs and thinning reduce yield, and each die is larger than a comparable DDR die. It also needs costly interposer packaging with limited factory capacity. Only three companies make it in volume (SK hynix, Samsung and Micron), and AI demand has kept supply tight. HBM4 moves the base die to a logic process, opening the door to custom base dies designed with the customer (Chapter 15).

Example 7.2: Checking the HBM table

  • HBM3: \(6.4 \times 1024 / 8 = 819.2\) GB/s, matching 819 GB/s.
  • HBM4 at 8 Gbps: \(8 \times 2048 / 8 = 2048\) GB/s, about 2 TB/s. Doubling the bus width halves the pin speed needed for a given bandwidth, which is an advantage because wires can then run slower.
  • Capacity: a 12-high HBM3E stack of 36 GB means \(36 \times 8 / 12 = 24\) Gb per die; a 16-high stack of 48 GB means 24 Gb dies again, and 64 GB means 32 Gb dies.

docs.title: 7.5 Specialty and historic DRAM
docs.text:
Beyond the four big families, DRAM has been adapted for special jobs.

RLDRAM (reduced-latency DRAM). RLDRAM uses smaller, more numerous banks and an SRAM-like interface with no need to manage rows, so a random access completes much sooner than in standard DRAM. It sits between QDR SRAM (faster, smaller) and DDR (larger, slower) in cost and performance, and is used mainly for packet buffers and lookup tables in network equipment.

eDRAM (embedded DRAM). eDRAM puts DRAM cells on the same die as logic (or in the same package), usually with a deep-trench or special capacitor. It gives several times the density of SRAM at somewhat higher latency, plus refresh. Examples are the large L3 caches in IBM POWER and IBM Z mainframe processors, the Intel Iris Pro graphics cache ("Crystal Well") and the 10 MB of eDRAM next to the Xbox 360 GPU. It is rare at the newest process nodes, where stacked SRAM has largely taken its place.

FPM and EDO DRAM. Fast Page Mode DRAM let the controller read several columns from an already-open row without repeating the row address. Extended Data Out DRAM kept output data valid while the next column address was supplied, overlapping the two steps. Both were asynchronous (no clock) and powered the PCs of the 1990s on SIMM modules before SDRAM replaced them.

RDRAM (Rambus DRAM). Rambus DRAM used a narrow, very fast packet-based bus with chips daisy-chained along the channel. It offered high bandwidth for its day but had high latency, high cost, heat and licensing disputes. It appeared in the Nintendo 64, the PlayStation 2 and early Pentium 4 PCs (RIMM modules) before DDR won the PC market.

XDR DRAM. XDR was Rambus's successor to RDRAM, using differential signalling and multiple transfers per clock for high per-pin bandwidth. Its best-known use was as the main memory of the Sony PlayStation 3, alongside GDDR3 for graphics.

VRAM, SGRAM and WRAM. The graphics cards of the 1990s used special DRAMs. VRAM was dual-ported: one port for the processor to draw into, and a serial port that streamed pixels to the display at the same time. SGRAM (synchronous graphics RAM) added features such as block writes to fill areas quickly, and evolved into GDDR. WRAM (window RAM) was a cheaper, faster dual-ported variant used in cards such as the Matrox Millennium.

docs.title: 7.6 Summary
docs.text:
• HBM stacks 8, 12 or 16 DRAM dies joined by TSVs on a base die and reaches the processor through a 1024-bit (HBM4: 2048-bit) bus on a silicon interposer.
  • A stack gives about 1.2 TB/s (HBM3E) to over 2 TB/s (HBM4); eight stacks give 8 to 10 TB/s, roughly 80 to 95 times a dual-channel desktop.
  • HBM costs several times more per gigabyte than DDR5 and is made by three companies.
  • The specialty DRAMs adapted the cell and interface for latency (RLDRAM), density next to logic (eDRAM), or graphics (VRAM, SGRAM); the Rambus designs lost to DDR.

docs.title: 7.7 Exercises
docs.text:
Exercise 7.1. Compute the bandwidth of one HBM2E stack at 3.2 Gbps per pin on a 1024-bit bus.

Answer

\(3.2 \times 1024 / 8 = 409.6\) GB/s, inside the 256 to 460 GB/s range for HBM2/2E.

Exercise 7.2. An accelerator has six HBM3E stacks at 9.6 Gbps. What is its total bandwidth and how many 12-high 36 GB stacks give its capacity?

Answer

Bandwidth \(= 6 \times 1228.8 = 7372.8\) GB/s, about 7.4 TB/s. Capacity \(= 6 \times 36 = 216\) GB.

Exercise 7.3. Why do HBM stacks sit on a silicon interposer instead of an ordinary circuit board?

Answer

A 1024-bit or 2048-bit interface per stack has thousands of wires, too many and too fine for an ordinary board. A silicon interposer has very fine wiring, so the thousands of wires fit and are only millimetres long, which also keeps the energy per bit low.

Exercise 7.4. Suppose a model needs all of its 140 GB of weights read once for every generated token, and the accelerator has 8 TB/s of memory bandwidth. What is the best-case token rate set by memory bandwidth alone?

Answer

\(8000 \text{ GB/s} / 140 \text{ GB} \approx 57\) tokens per second at most. This is a supposed example to show why bandwidth limits text generation; real rates are lower.

Exercise 7.5. Match each memory to its niche: eDRAM, RLDRAM, SGRAM, RDRAM. (a) network packet buffers; (b) large caches next to a processor core; (c) graphics cards of the 1990s that evolved into GDDR; (d) a narrow packet-based bus used by the Nintendo 64.

Answer

eDRAM: (b). RLDRAM: (a). SGRAM: (c). RDRAM: (d).

docs.title: Chapter 6: LPDDR and GDDR
docs.text: DDR is built for capacity and cost. Two other DRAM families keep the same cells but change the interface to serve a different goal. LPDDR (low-power DDR) minimises the energy spent per bit and lives in phones, thin laptops, cars and, increasingly, AI servers. GDDR (graphics DDR) maximises the speed of every pin for graphics cards and game consoles. This chapter explains what each does differently, follows each family through its generations, and works through the bandwidth arithmetic of the newest parts.

docs.title: 6.1 How LPDDR differs from DDR
docs.text:
LPDDR is the DRAM inside phones, tablets, most thin laptops, Apple Silicon Macs, cars and, increasingly, AI servers. It uses the same DRAM cells as DDR but a very different interface, tuned to save energy.

  • Narrow channels. LPDDR4 and LPDDR5 use 16-bit channels (LPDDR6 uses 24-bit channels made of two 12-bit sub-channels). A system gangs several channels together to get a wide bus, for example 64 or 128 bits in a laptop.
  • Soldered and close to the processor. Chips are soldered on the board, placed in the same package as the processor, or stacked on top of it (PoP, package-on-package). Short traces need less drive strength and allow high speeds at low power.
  • Low I/O voltage. LPDDR4X cut the I/O voltage to 0.6 V, and later generations go lower still, which greatly reduces the energy per bit moved.
  • Aggressive power states. Deep power-down and self-refresh modes let the memory sip power when the device is idle; partial-array self-refresh keeps only the needed part of memory alive.
  • DVFS (dynamic voltage and frequency scaling) lets the system lower the memory voltage and clock when full speed is not needed.

The trade-off is that LPDDR cannot normally be upgraded and has historically offered less capacity per channel than DDR. The LPCAMM2 and SOCAMM module formats (Chapter 8) remove the first limitation.

docs.title: 6.2 LPDDR3 (2012)
docs.text: LPDDR3 ran at 1600 to 2133 MT/s and powered the smartphones and tablets of the early 2010s. It introduced on-die termination options and write levelling to LPDDR. It is now legacy, found only in older devices.

docs.title: 6.3 LPDDR4 and LPDDR4X (2014 and 2017)
docs.text: LPDDR4 reorganised each die into two independent 16-bit channels and reached 3200 MT/s, later 4266 MT/s. LPDDR4X (2017) kept the same core but cut the I/O voltage from 1.1 V to 0.6 V, saving a large share of interface power. Both remain very common in budget phones, single-board computers such as many Raspberry Pi models, TVs and automotive systems, because they are cheap and well supported.

docs.title: 6.4 LPDDR5 (2019)
docs.text: LPDDR5 reached 6400 MT/s. It added bank groups (as in DDR4) for high-speed operation, a deep sleep mode for lower idle power, and DVFS support with a lower core-voltage mode at reduced speed. It also introduced a separate write-clock scheme for the data pins. LPDDR5 is now typical of mid-range phones and laptops.

docs.title: 6.5 LPDDR5X (2021)
docs.text: LPDDR5X extended the LPDDR5 design to 8533 MT/s and, in newer parts, around 9600 to 10,700 MT/s, the highest low-power DRAM speed shipping in volume in 2026. It is the memory in current flagship phones, Apple Silicon Macs, thin laptops and Nvidia's Grace server CPU. Equalisation and improved signalling make the higher speeds possible on short, carefully designed channels.

docs.title: 6.6 LPDDR6 (2025 standard, arriving 2026)
docs.text:
JEDEC published the LPDDR6 standard, JESD209-6, in 2025. Its biggest change is the channel: each 24-bit channel is made of two 12-bit sub-channels, and the extra width carries metadata bits that can be used for ECC and other information alongside the data. Speeds start around 10,667 MT/s with a path to about 14,400 MT/s. LPDDR6 also adds an efficiency mode that lets one sub-channel handle traffic while the other sleeps, and PRAC (per-row activation counting) to defend against rowhammer attacks, in which repeated activation of one row flips bits in its neighbours. First devices were arriving in 2026.

Example 6.1: The numbers inside an LPDDR6 channel

The standard's figures fit together as follows.

  1. A burst of 24 transfers on one 12-bit sub-channel moves \(24 \times 12 = 288\) bits.
  2. Of these, 256 bits are data (32 bytes) and the other \(288 - 256 = 32\) bits are metadata.
  3. One 24-bit channel at 10,667 MT/s moves \(24 \times 10{,}667 / 8 / 1000 = 32.0\) GB/s raw; at 14,400 MT/s, \(24 \times 14{,}400 / 8 / 1000 = 43.2\) GB/s, the "about 43 GB/s" of the standard's raw figure.
  4. An LPDDR5X channel (16 bits) at 10.7 Gbps gives \(16 \times 10{,}700 / 8 / 1000 = 21.4\) GB/s.

"Raw" counts all pins, so the metadata share of each burst, 32 of 288 bits or 11.1 per cent, is not available as plain data.

docs.text: Generation Year Speed (MT/s) Key change Typical use (2026) LPDDR3 2012 1600–2133 None to note Legacy LPDDR4/4X 2014/2017 3200–4266 4X cut I/O voltage to 0.6 V Budget phones, single-board computers LPDDR5 2019 6400 Bank groups, deep sleep Mid-range LPDDR5X 2021 8533–10,700 Highest low-power speed shipping in volume Current flagship LPDDR6 2025 (JESD209-6) 10,667–14,400 24-bit channels (2 × 12-bit sub-channels), metadata bits for ECC, efficiency mode, PRAC rowhammer protection Arriving 2026

docs.title: 6.8 Why GDDR is different
docs.text:
GDDR is built for one job: moving as many bits per second through each pin as possible, at a reasonable price, for graphics cards and game consoles.

A GPU has thousands of cores working on huge textures and frame buffers, so it needs far more bandwidth than a CPU, but it tolerates higher latency, because it can switch to other work while waiting. GDDR exploits this by running each pin much faster than DDR, tens of gigabits per second instead of a few, at the cost of higher power per chip and somewhat higher latency. Each GDDR chip has a 32-bit interface (split internally into narrower channels), and the chips are soldered in a ring around the GPU on short, point-to-point traces, with no modules or slots. A GPU with a 256-bit bus uses eight chips; a 384-bit bus uses twelve.

Signalling has evolved to keep raising per-pin speed (Section 3.4). GDDR5, GDDR5X and GDDR6 use two-level NRZ. GDDR6X, developed by Micron with Nvidia, switched to four-level PAM4, sending 2 bits per symbol. GDDR7 adopted three-level PAM3 (1.5 bits per symbol), which gives better noise margins than PAM4 while still beating NRZ.

docs.title: 6.9 The GDDR generations
docs.text:
GDDR5 (2008). About 4 to 8 Gbps per pin; it dominated graphics for nearly a decade: Nvidia GTX 900 and most GTX 1000 cards, the AMD Radeon cards of the period and the PlayStation 4, which used 8 GB of GDDR5 as unified memory for both CPU and GPU. It introduced separate clocks for commands and data, and link training to tune timing at start-up.

GDDR5X (2016). It doubled the prefetch of GDDR5 to reach about 10 to 14 Gbps while staying with NRZ. It had a short life, used mainly by Micron and Nvidia, most famously in the GTX 1080 and 1080 Ti.

GDDR6 (2018). It split each chip into two independent 16-bit channels and reached 14 to 20 Gbps with NRZ. It became the industry's workhorse: Nvidia RTX 20-series and many RTX 30 and 40 cards, AMD RX 6000 and 7000, the PlayStation 5 and the Xbox Series X and S. It remains the budget choice for graphics in 2026.

GDDR6X (2020). A Micron and Nvidia collaboration rather than a broad JEDEC standard, it used PAM4 signalling to reach about 19 to 24 Gbps. It powered high-end Nvidia cards such as the RTX 3080, 3090 and 4090. PAM4's smaller voltage steps demanded very careful board design.

GDDR7 (2024 to 2025). GDDR7 (JEDEC JESD239, 2024) uses PAM3 and splits each chip into four channels. First products run at 28 to 32 Gbps per pin, with vendor roadmaps reaching towards 48 Gbps. It is used in the Nvidia RTX 50 series, and also adds stronger error handling and options for lower-power operation.

Generation Year Speed per pin Signalling Example products GDDR5 2008 4–8 Gbps NRZ GTX 900/1000, PS4 GDDR5X 2016 10–14 Gbps NRZ GTX 1080 GDDR6 2018 14–20 Gbps NRZ RTX 20/30/40 (some), RX 6000/7000, PS5, Xbox Series GDDR6X 2020 19–24 Gbps PAM4 RTX 3080/3090/4090 (Micron and Nvidia only) GDDR7 2024–25 28–32 Gbps, roadmap to 48 PAM3 RTX 50 series

Example 6.2: GPU memory bandwidth

For a chip with 32 data pins, bandwidth (GB/s) is the per-pin rate in Gbps times 32 divided by 8, or four times the per-pin rate.

  1. One GDDR7 chip at 32 Gbps: \(32 \times 32 / 8 = 128\) GB/s.
  2. A card with a 512-bit bus uses \(512/32 = 16\) chips. At 28 Gbps the bus delivers \(28 \times 512 / 8 = 1792\) GB/s.
  3. For comparison, a 256-bit card with GDDR6 chips at 16 Gbps (a value inside the 14 to 20 Gbps range) uses 8 chips and delivers \(16 \times 256 / 8 = 512\) GB/s, about 17 times the 25.6 GB/s of a single DDR4-3200 channel.

docs.title: 6.10 Summary
docs.text:
• LPDDR keeps DRAM cells but narrows the channel, shortens the wires, lowers the I/O voltage and adds deep power states, to minimise energy per bit.
  • LPDDR4X cut I/O voltage to 0.6 V; LPDDR5X reaches 8533 to 10,700 MT/s; LPDDR6 uses 24-bit channels of two 12-bit sub-channels with metadata bits and PRAC.
  • GDDR maximises per-pin speed (tens of Gbps) for graphics, soldered point-to-point around the GPU, tolerating higher latency.
  • GDDR6X (PAM4) and GDDR7 (PAM3) raise the data rate without raising the symbol rate in proportion.
  • Bandwidth for a 32-pin GDDR chip is four times the per-pin rate in Gbps; a 512-bit card at 28 Gbps reaches 1792 GB/s.

docs.title: 6.11 Exercises
docs.text:
Exercise 6.1. A thin laptop has LPDDR5X-8533 on a 128-bit bus (eight 16-bit channels). Find its peak bandwidth.

Answer

\(8533 \times 128 / 8 / 1000 = 136.5\) GB/s.

Exercise 6.2. A GPU has a 192-bit memory bus built from GDDR6 chips with 32 data pins each, running at 18 Gbps. How many chips does it have and what is its peak bandwidth?

Answer

\(192/32 = 6\) chips. Bandwidth \(= 18 \times 192 / 8 = 432\) GB/s.

Exercise 6.3. Why can a GPU tolerate GDDR's higher latency, while a CPU prefers DDR or LPDDR?

Answer

A GPU has thousands of cores and can switch to other work while a memory request is outstanding, so it hides latency with parallelism. A CPU has few threads and stalls when waiting for data, so it values low latency, and its memory also needs large capacity (DDR) or low power (LPDDR).

Exercise 6.4. Which of these is an LPDDR feature and which a GDDR feature: PoP stacking; PAM3 signalling; deep power-down; 0.6 V I/O; a 384-bit bus of soldered chips?

Answer

LPDDR: PoP stacking, deep power-down, 0.6 V I/O (LPDDR4X and later). GDDR: PAM3 signalling (GDDR7) and a 384-bit bus of soldered chips (twelve chips around the GPU).

Exercise 6.5. Explain how LPDDR6's 288-bit burst on a 12-bit sub-channel splits into data and metadata, and what the metadata can be used for.

Answer

The burst is 24 transfers of 12 bits, 288 bits. 256 bits are data (32 bytes) and 32 bits are metadata, which can be used for ECC and other information alongside the data.

docs.title: Chapter 8: Memory Module Form Factors
docs.text: The same DRAM chips can be packaged in very different ways. The module format decides capacity, speed, upgradeability and reliability as much as the chips do. This chapter surveys the formats in use in 2026, from the unbuffered DIMM of the desktop to the compression-mounted modules of thin laptops and AI servers and the CXL expanders that add memory beyond the slots, and then lists the helper chips that sit on a module beside the DRAM.

docs.title: 8.1 UDIMM (unbuffered DIMM)
docs.text: The standard desktop module: the memory chips connect directly to the motherboard's memory controller with nothing in between. DDR5 UDIMMs have 288 pins. They are cheap and low in latency, but each channel supports only a limited number of chips.

docs.title: 8.2 SO-DIMM (small outline DIMM)
docs.text: A shorter UDIMM for laptops, mini PCs and some embedded boards (262 pins for DDR5). It is upgradeable but takes board space and limits speed compared with soldered memory.

docs.title: 8.3 CUDIMM and CSODIMM (clocked)
docs.text: These are DDR5 UDIMMs and SO-DIMMs with an added clock driver (CKD) chip that cleans up and re-drives the clock signal on the module. This helps reach DDR5-8000 and beyond on desktops and laptops, where an unbuffered clock becomes too noisy.

docs.title: 8.4 RDIMM (registered DIMM)
docs.text: Server modules with a registering clock driver (RCD) that buffers the command and address signals. The controller drives one load per module instead of every chip, so many more chips and much larger capacities fit on a channel. The price is a little latency. RDIMMs are almost always used with side-band ECC.

docs.title: 8.5 LRDIMM (load-reduced DIMM)
docs.text: An LRDIMM goes further than an RDIMM by also buffering the data signals with data buffer chips, allowing even higher capacity per channel. With DDR5, very large RDIMMs have made LRDIMMs less common.

docs.title: 8.6 MRDIMM (multiplexed-rank DIMM)
docs.text: A DDR5 server module that runs two ranks at once and multiplexes them onto the bus at double speed, using special buffer chips. The first generation reaches 8800 MT/s, about 40 per cent more bandwidth than standard RDIMMs, and a second generation targets 12,800 MT/s. It needs processor support (for example, recent Intel Xeon platforms).

docs.title: 8.7 CAMM2 and LPCAMM2
docs.text: Compression-attached memory modules: instead of an edge connector in a slot, a flat module is screwed down onto a pad of contacts on the board. This shortens the signal path, saves height and allows higher speeds. CAMM2 carries DDR5; LPCAMM2 carries LPDDR5X, giving laptops LPDDR speed and efficiency in a replaceable module.

docs.title: 8.8 SOCAMM
docs.text: A compact compression-mounted module carrying LPDDR5X, developed for AI servers with Nvidia's Grace and Vera CPUs. It brings LPDDR's high bandwidth per watt to servers while keeping memory serviceable; a second generation, SOCAMM2, was being standardised in 2026.

docs.title: 8.9 CXL memory module
docs.text: DRAM (usually DDR5) placed behind a CXL (Compute Express Link) controller, which talks to the processor over PCIe-style wires instead of a DDR bus. It is packaged as E3.S drives or add-in cards and adds capacity beyond the DIMM slots, at a latency roughly comparable to a remote processor socket's memory. With CXL switches, memory can be pooled and shared among servers. In the hierarchy of Figure 1.1 it is the tier between local DRAM and storage.

docs.title: 8.10 NVDIMM-N
docs.text: A DIMM carrying DRAM plus flash and a backup power source (a supercapacitor or battery). It runs at DRAM speed; if power fails, the module copies its DRAM contents to flash and restores them at the next boot. It is used for databases and storage systems that must never lose recent writes, and is now a niche product.

docs.title: 8.11 What else sits on a module
docs.text:
A module is more than DRAM chips. The helper components, which Chapters 11 to 14 return to in detail, are:

Component Function Where SPD EEPROM / SPD hub Stores the module's specifications (size, speeds, timings, including XMP/EXPO overclocking profiles); read by the BIOS at boot All modules PMIC Converts the 5 V (desktop) or 12 V (server) input to the DRAM voltages; moved onto the DIMM with DDR5 DDR5 Temperature sensor Reports module temperature so the system can adjust refresh and cooling DDR5, servers RCD Buffers command, address and clock signals RDIMMs Data buffers Buffer the data signals LRDIMMs Decoupling capacitors Supply instantaneous current and keep supply voltage steady All Termination resistors Absorb signal reflections on the module All

Many consumer modules also add a metal heat spreader, sometimes RGB LEDs with their own small controller, and a printed label with part number, capacity, speed and timings.

docs.title: 8.12 Module summary
docs.text:
Module Key feature Typical use UDIMM Unbuffered, direct connection Desktops SO-DIMM Small unbuffered module Laptops, mini PCs CUDIMM / CSODIMM Clock driver chip on module DDR5-8000+ desktops and laptops RDIMM Registered command/address via RCD; ECC Servers, workstations LRDIMM Data buffers as well as RCD Very high-capacity servers MRDIMM Multiplexed ranks; 8800 MT/s gen 1, 12,800 gen 2 Bandwidth-heavy servers (HPC, AI) CAMM2 / LPCAMM2 Compression-mounted, thin, fast Laptops SOCAMM LPDDR5X server module AI servers (Nvidia Grace/Vera) CXL memory module DRAM behind a CXL/PCIe link (E3.S or add-in card) Server memory expansion and pooling NVDIMM-N DRAM + flash + backup capacitor Storage and database servers

The other physical forms in which RAM is found are not modules at all: soldered LPDDR in phones and thin laptops; package-on-package, where the DRAM package sits on top of the processor; HBM on a silicon interposer; and embedded SRAM, inside processors, graphics chips and almost every other chip.

Example 8.1: Reading a module's label

A server memory label reads "DDR5 RDIMM 1Rx4 ECC 32 GB, 4800 MT/s". The notation "1Rx4" means one rank built from x4 chips (each with 4 data pins).

  1. One rank must fill the channel width: with ECC, \(2 \times (32 + 8) = 80\) bits.
  2. With x4 chips: \(80 / 4 = 20\) chips.
  3. Data capacity with 16 Gb chips: 16 data chips \(\times\) 2 GB \(= 32\) GB, and the other four chips hold the ECC bits.
  4. The "R" in RDIMM tells us there is an RCD, so the processor sees one command load per module.

An MRDIMM at 8800 MT/s compared with an RDIMM at 6400 MT/s offers \(8800/6400 = 1.375\) times the data rate, "about 40 per cent more".

docs.title: 8.13 Summary
docs.text:
• The module format decides capacity, speed, upgradeability and reliability.
  • UDIMM and SO-DIMM connect chips directly; CUDIMM adds a clock driver for 8000+ MT/s; RDIMM adds an RCD and ECC for servers; LRDIMM buffers data too; MRDIMM multiplexes two ranks for 8800 MT/s and up.
  • CAMM2, LPCAMM2 and SOCAMM replace the edge connector with a screwed-down flat module; CXL modules add capacity over PCIe-style wires; NVDIMM-N keeps DRAM data across power loss using flash and a backup supply.
  • Every module carries helper parts: SPD, PMIC, temperature sensors, decoupling capacitors, termination, and, for RDIMMs, an RCD.

docs.title: 8.14 Exercises
docs.text:
Exercise 8.1. Why does an RDIMM allow more chips per channel than a UDIMM?

Answer

The RCD buffers command and address signals, so the memory controller drives one load per module instead of one per chip. Less loading means more chips and higher capacity per channel, at the cost of a little latency.

Exercise 8.2. Choose a module type: (a) a thin laptop that must be upgradeable and fast; (b) a gaming desktop at DDR5-8000; (c) a database server that must not lose recent writes; (d) a server needing more memory than its slots provide.

Answer

(a) LPCAMM2 (LPDDR speed in a replaceable module) or a DDR5 SO-DIMM. (b) CUDIMM. (c) NVDIMM-N (DRAM backed by flash and a supercapacitor or battery). (d) A CXL memory module.

Exercise 8.3. A 2Rx8 DDR5 non-ECC UDIMM uses 16 Gb chips. How many chips does it have and what is its capacity?

Answer

Each rank has \(64/8 = 8\) chips, and two ranks give 16 chips. Capacity \(= 16 \times 16\) Gb \(= 256\) Gb \(= 32\) GB.

Exercise 8.4. What do an MRDIMM and a CUDIMM each add to a DDR5 module, and what problem does each solve?

Answer

A CUDIMM adds a clock driver (CKD) chip that re-drives a clean clock, so unbuffered desktop modules can reach DDR5-8000 and beyond. An MRDIMM adds special buffer chips that run two ranks at once and multiplex them onto the bus at double speed, giving about 40 per cent more bandwidth than a standard RDIMM.

Exercise 8.5. List four helper components found on a DDR5 RDIMM and say what each does.

Answer

SPD hub (stores the module's specifications for the BIOS), PMIC (converts the supplied 12 V into the DRAM voltages), RCD (buffers command, address and clock) and temperature sensors (report temperature so the system can adjust refresh and cooling). Decoupling capacitors and termination resistors are also present.

docs.title: Chapter 9: Non-volatile and Emerging RAM
docs.text: These memories keep data without power while still allowing fast, byte-level access. None has replaced DRAM, but several are now standard as embedded memory in microcontrollers and specialised products. This chapter explains how each stores a bit (as a magnetic orientation, a polarisation, a filament, a phase or a nanotube contact), what each is good at, and where each is used or has been tried.

docs.title: 9.1 MRAM (magnetoresistive RAM)
docs.text:
MRAM stores a bit in a magnetic tunnel junction (MTJ): two magnetic layers separated by a thin insulator. One layer is fixed; the other can point the same way (low resistance, a 0) or the opposite way (high resistance, a 1). Reading senses the resistance; writing flips the free layer.

STT-MRAM (spin-transfer torque) flips the free layer by passing current through the junction. SOT-MRAM (spin-orbit torque) uses a separate write path for faster, longer-lasting writes and is still largely in research.

MRAM has very high endurance, is naturally immune to radiation upsets and is offered as embedded memory by major foundries. Uses: embedded code and data memory in microcontrollers, industrial and automotive chips, and aerospace systems.

docs.title: 9.2 FeRAM / FRAM (ferroelectric RAM)
docs.text:
FeRAM looks like a DRAM cell, but the capacitor is filled with a ferroelectric material whose internal polarisation stays pointing up or down after power is removed. Writes are fast and low in energy, and endurance is very high, on the order of \(10^{14}\) cycles or more. Capacities are small, and reading is destructive, so the cell is rewritten after each read, as in DRAM. Newer hafnium-oxide ferroelectrics may let FeRAM scale further.

Uses: smart meters, medical devices, data loggers and microcontrollers such as the TI MSP430FR family.

Example 9.1: How long does a data logger last?

A data logger writes one record to the same FRAM location once per second. With an endurance of \(10^{14}\) write cycles:

  1. One year has about \(365 \times 24 \times 3600 = 3.15 \times 10^{7}\) seconds, so about \(3.15 \times 10^{7}\) writes per year.
  2. \(10^{14} / 3.15 \times 10^{7} \approx 3.2 \times 10^{6}\) years.

Endurance is therefore no practical limit for this job. Flash, which wears out after a limited number of writes and is written in large pages, would need wear levelling to survive the same workload.

docs.title: 9.3 ReRAM / RRAM (resistive RAM)
docs.text:
ReRAM stores a bit as the resistance of a thin oxide layer. Applying a voltage forms or breaks a tiny conductive filament through the oxide, switching between low and high resistance. Cells are simple and can be built between metal layers above the transistors. Endurance is lower than MRAM's.

Uses: embedded non-volatile memory in microcontrollers at advanced nodes, and research into in-memory computing, where arrays of resistive cells perform multiply-accumulate operations for neural networks directly in the array.

docs.title: 9.4 PCM and 3D XPoint (phase-change memory)
docs.text: PCM uses a chalcogenide glass that can be switched by heat pulses between an amorphous state (high resistance) and a crystalline state (low resistance). Intel and Micron's 3D XPoint, sold as Intel Optane, used a related technology in SSDs and in persistent memory DIMMs that sat between DRAM and flash. Despite good performance, Optane was discontinued in 2022 because it could not compete on cost. Phase-change memory still appears as embedded memory in some automotive microcontrollers.

docs.title: 9.5 NRAM (nanotube RAM)
docs.text: NRAM stores bits using a layer of carbon nanotubes that are pushed into or out of contact with each other, changing the resistance. It promises speed, endurance and tolerance of heat and radiation, but remains experimental, with no mainstream products as of 2026.

docs.title: 9.6 Non-volatile RAM summary
docs.text:
Type How it stores a bit Strengths Where used MRAM (STT/SOT) Magnetic orientation in a magnetic tunnel junction Fast, very high endurance, radiation-tolerant Embedded MCU memory, industrial, aerospace FeRAM / FRAM Polarisation of a ferroelectric capacitor Very low write energy, fast writes, high endurance Smart meters, medical, TI MSP430FR ReRAM / RRAM Conductive filament in an oxide (resistance) Simple, dense, built between metal layers Embedded NVM, in-memory compute research PCM / 3D XPoint Amorphous versus crystalline phase (resistance) Byte-addressable, denser than DRAM Intel Optane (discontinued 2022), some automotive MCUs NRAM Carbon nanotubes in contact or apart Potentially fast and robust Experimental

The processes on which these are built differ from those of DRAM. Embedded MRAM is typically offered at 28, 22, 16 and 12 nm, moving to 14 and 8 nm; standalone MRAM at 28 to 40 nm; FeRAM at about 130 nm; embedded ReRAM at 40, 28 and 22 nm. Embedded MRAM is available on the GlobalFoundries 22FDX process alongside SRAM (Chapter 16).

docs.title: 9.7 Summary
docs.text:
• Non-volatile RAMs keep data without power and allow byte access; none has replaced DRAM, but several are standard embedded memories.
  • MRAM stores a bit as a magnetic orientation (high endurance, radiation-tolerant); FeRAM as ferroelectric polarisation (very low write energy, around \(10^{14}\) cycles); ReRAM as a filament's resistance; PCM as amorphous or crystalline phase; NRAM as nanotube contact.
  • Optane, the best-known PCM product, was discontinued in 2022 because of cost; NRAM remains experimental.

docs.title: 9.8 Exercises
docs.text:
Exercise 9.1. For each memory, name the physical property that represents the bit: MRAM, FeRAM, ReRAM, PCM.

Answer

MRAM: the magnetic orientation of the free layer in a magnetic tunnel junction (resistance low or high). FeRAM: the polarisation of a ferroelectric capacitor. ReRAM: the resistance of an oxide, set by forming or breaking a conductive filament. PCM: the phase, amorphous (high resistance) or crystalline (low resistance).

Exercise 9.2. A smart meter must store a counter updated every 10 seconds for 20 years. How many writes is that, and is an endurance of \(10^{14}\) cycles enough?

Answer

Seconds in 20 years \(\approx 20 \times 3.15 \times 10^{7} = 6.3 \times 10^{8}\); one write every 10 s gives \(6.3 \times 10^{7}\) writes, far below \(10^{14}\). Endurance is more than sufficient, by a factor of about \(1.6 \times 10^{6}\).

Exercise 9.3. Why was Intel Optane discontinued although its performance was good?

Answer

It could not compete on cost. It had sat between DRAM and flash in persistent-memory DIMMs and SSDs, but good performance alone did not make up for the cost.

Exercise 9.4. Which non-volatile RAM would you consider for (a) a spacecraft microcontroller's code memory; (b) in-memory neural-network computing research; (c) a medical device logging data frequently at very low energy?

Answer

(a) MRAM, because it is radiation-tolerant and endurant. (b) ReRAM, whose resistive arrays can perform multiply-accumulate directly. (c) FeRAM, with very low write energy and very high endurance.

Exercise 9.5. Explain what "destructive read" means for FeRAM and why DRAM shares the property.

Answer

Reading an FeRAM cell disturbs the polarisation that stores the bit, so the controller must rewrite the value after every read. A DRAM cell shares its charge with the bitline when read, which drains the capacitor, so DRAM also rewrites the row after reading (Section 2.3).

docs.title: Chapter 13: Power: Clean, Steady Voltage for Twenty Chips
docs.text: Memory chips draw sudden gulps of current. The module must convert the motherboard's 12 V into precise low voltages and keep them steady during every gulp. This chapter follows the power from the edge connector: the power-management chip that makes four voltages from 12 V, the budget of currents and watts under the data-sheet limits (with an open problem that the numbers revealed), and the capacitors that act as small local water tanks. A worked analysis of the power-delivery network shows how many capacitors are enough, and why.

docs.title: 13.1 The power tree
docs.text:
