A DDR5 module carries its own power-management IC (PMIC), which moved onto the DIMM with DDR5. In the project it is the Richtek RTQ5119A, which has four switching regulators and three small linear regulators and is about 90 per cent efficient. It takes 12 V from the slot (the bulk input, with 3.3 V for management) and produces the voltages the chips need.

Output Voltage Current limit What it powers VDD 1.1 V up to 7 A (two regulators working together) The chip core VDDQ 1.1 V 3.5 A The data pins and the RCD VPP 1.8 V 3.5 A The pumps that drive the wordlines

VPP is higher than the core voltage because the wordline must be driven well above the supply to switch the access transistor on fully.

docs.title: 13.2 The current budget
docs.text:
Using the data sheets' worst-case currents, the project tabulated what each rail draws in three states and the total power of the module.

State VDD VDDQ VPP Module power Idle 1.5 A 1.8 A 0.2 A 4.5 W Reading flat out 4.3 A 4.6 A 0.2 A 11.4 W Writing flat out 5.1 A 5.6 A 0.5 A 14.1 W

Example 13.1: From currents to module power

The module power is the output power of the three rails divided by the PMIC's efficiency (about 0.9).

For writing flat out:

  1. VDD: \(5.1\ \text{A} \times 1.1\ \text{V} = 5.61\) W.
  2. VDDQ: \(5.6 \times 1.1 = 6.16\) W.
  3. VPP: \(0.5 \times 1.8 = 0.90\) W.
  4. Sum \(= 12.67\) W at the outputs. Divide by 0.9: \(12.67/0.9 = 14.1\) W, matching the table.

For idle: \(1.5 \times 1.1 + 1.8 \times 1.1 + 0.2 \times 1.8 = 3.99\) W, and \(3.99/0.9 = 4.43\) W, which matches 4.5 W within rounding. For reading: \(4.3 \times 1.1 + 4.6 \times 1.1 + 0.2 \times 1.8 = 10.15\) W, and \(10.15/0.9 = 11.3\) W against 11.4 W in the table, again within the rounding of the currents.

At 12 V the writing state draws about \(14.1/12 = 1.2\) A from the slot.

An open problem, found by the numbers

At the data sheet's maximum currents, VDDQ needs about 5.6 A, but its regulator is rated 3.5 A: 60 per cent more than the PMIC can supply (\(5.6/3.5 = 1.6\)). The reading state (4.6 A) also exceeds it. Real modules ship with this kind of PMIC, so typical currents must be much lower than the worst-case maximums. Resolving the question needs the vendor's typical-current data or a bigger PMIC. The project keeps a test that fails on purpose until this is fixed, so that the problem cannot be forgotten.

This is a good example of a design review turning a spreadsheet into a question. A maximum-current figure on a data sheet is a limit, not a typical value, and designing to the limit can over-constrain a design while ignoring the limit can under-design it. The honest answer is "not resolved yet", and the project says so.

docs.title: 13.3 Decoupling: capacitors as water tanks
docs.text:
The power chip is too slow to react to a gulp of current lasting nanoseconds. So the board places capacitors everywhere: small local tanks that cover the gulp until the regulator catches up. Big capacitors handle slow changes, and small ones handle fast changes.

Engineers check the impedance of the power network seen by the chip across frequency. If the chip suddenly draws an extra current \(\Delta I\) and the network has impedance \(Z\) at that frequency, the supply dips by \(\Delta I \cdot Z\). To keep the dip within an allowed ripple \(\Delta V\), the impedance must stay below the target

\[Z_{target} = \frac{\Delta V}{\Delta I}\]

at every frequency for which the board is responsible. In the project the target is 8.75 mΩ (3 per cent ripple at a 50 per cent load step). For the 1.1 V rail, 3 per cent is 33 mV, so the target corresponds to a load step of \(33\ \text{mV}/8.75\ \text{m}\Omega \approx 3.8\) A.

The course's model describes each capacitor as a capacitance in series with a resistance (ESR) and an inductance (ESL), and the PMIC as 2 mΩ in series with 3 nH. The parameters used are:

Capacitor Effective capacitance ESR ESL 22 µF bulk 60 per cent of 22 µF 3 mΩ 0.8 nH 1 µF 70 per cent of 1 µF 10 mΩ 0.6 nH 100 nF 80 per cent of 100 nF 30 mΩ 0.5 nH

The reduction of the effective capacitance reflects the way real capacitors lose capacitance under bias. The model adds the admittances (the reciprocals of the impedances) of all parallel branches, inverts the sum, and checks the impedance up to 100 MHz; above that the package takes over.

Example 13.2: How many 22 µF capacitors?

With 20 capacitors of 1 µF and 20 of 100 nF fixed, vary the number of 22 µF capacitors. The worst impedance below 100 MHz, from the model above, is:

22 µF capacitors Worst impedance (mΩ) At frequency Against 8.75 mΩ 0 79.5 738 kHz fail 4 17.9 346 kHz fail 8 11.4 257 kHz fail 10 9.7 237 kHz fail 12 8.5 213 kHz pass 14 7.6 201 kHz pass 16 6.9 186 kHz pass

Ten fail and twelve pass. The project uses 14, which gives \((8.75 - 7.63)/8.75 = 12.8\) per cent margin, "about 13 per cent". The first design had only 4 large capacitors on VDD, and the analysis showed the impedance peaking above the target at a few hundred kilohertz, the caution this table shows. The fix was 14 × 22 µF.

Figure 13.1. Impedance against frequency for 4, 10 and 14 large capacitors on a log-log plot, with a dashed target line at 8.75 milliohms: only the 14-capacitor curve stays below the target across the band

In Figure 13.1 the peak near 200 to 350 kHz is the one that matters: it appears where the regulator's inductance meets the capacitance of the bulk capacitors (a parallel resonance), and only enough bulk capacitance pushes it below the target. The lower peaks at several MHz belong to the smaller capacitors.

docs.title: 13.4 Summary
docs.text:
• One PMIC makes VDD (1.1 V, up to 7 A), VDDQ (1.1 V, 3.5 A) and VPP (1.8 V, 3.5 A) from 12 V at about 90 per cent efficiency.
  • Worst-case module power is 4.5 W idle, 11.4 W reading and 14.1 W writing; these follow from the rail currents divided by the efficiency.
  • VDDQ's worst-case 5.6 A exceeds its 3.5 A regulator: an open problem left visible by a deliberately failing test.
  • Decoupling capacitors serve as local tanks. The target impedance is \(\Delta V/\Delta I\); for this module it is 8.75 mΩ, which needs 12 or more of the 22 µF capacitors (the project uses 14).

docs.title: 13.5 Exercises
docs.text:
Exercise 13.1. Compute the module power when reading flat out, given currents 4.3 A (VDD), 4.6 A (VDDQ) and 0.2 A (VPP) and an efficiency of 0.9. Compare it with the table.

Answer

Output power \(= 4.3 \times 1.1 + 4.6 \times 1.1 + 0.2 \times 1.8 = 4.73 + 5.06 + 0.36 = 10.15\) W. Input power \(= 10.15/0.9 = 11.28\) W, against 11.4 W in the table: the 1 per cent difference comes from the rounding of the currents.

Exercise 13.2. A different rail has a ripple allowance of 5 per cent on 1.1 V and must tolerate a 4 A load step. What target impedance does it need?

Answer

\(\Delta V = 0.05 \times 1.1 = 55\) mV, so \(Z_{target} = 0.055/4 = 13.75\) mΩ.

Exercise 13.3. The VDDQ regulator is rated 3.5 A. By how much does the data sheet's worst-case current exceed the rating when reading (4.6 A) and when writing (5.6 A)?

Answer

Reading: \(4.6 - 3.5 = 1.1\) A over, or 31 per cent above the rating (\(4.6/3.5 = 1.31\)). Writing: \(5.6 - 3.5 = 2.1\) A over, or 60 per cent above the rating. Idle (1.8 A) is within the rating.

Exercise 13.4. Why is the worst-case impedance peak in Figure 13.1 at a few hundred kilohertz and not at several megahertz?

Answer

At low frequency the regulator's inductance (3 nH and its small resistance) resonates against the capacitance of the bulk capacitors, and with too few bulk capacitors the resonance rises above the target. Higher peaks at MHz frequencies are formed by the smaller capacitors' ESL and capacitance, and these are less critical because many capacitors of those values are in parallel.

Exercise 13.5 (Assignment 9: size the decoupling capacitors). Model each capacitor as \(C\) + ESR + ESL in series, and the PMIC as 2 mΩ + 3 nH. Add 20 × 1 µF and 20 × 100 nF, then vary the number of 22 µF capacitors. Plot \(|Z|\) from 10 kHz to 100 MHz against the 8.75 mΩ target.

Answer 

import numpy as np

CAPS = {  # (effective C, ESR, ESL)
    "bulk": (22e-6 * 0.6, 0.003, 0.8e-9),
    "mid":  (1e-6 * 0.7, 0.010, 0.6e-9),
    "hf":   (100e-9 * 0.8, 0.030, 0.5e-9),
}

def z_abs(f, n):
    w = 2 * np.pi * f
    y = 1 / (0.002 + 1j * w * 3e-9)                    # PMIC branch
    y += 1j * w * 0.9e-9                               # fixed small capacitance in the course model
    for name, count in n.items():
        c, esr, esl = CAPS[name]
        y += count / (esr + 1j * (w * esl - 1 / (w * c)))
    return 1 / abs(y)

f = np.logspace(4, 8, 400)
for nb in (10, 12, 14):
    worst = max(z_abs(x, {"bulk": nb, "mid": 20, "hf": 20}) for x in f)
    print(nb, round(worst * 1000, 2), "mOhm", "pass" if worst <= 8.75e-3 else "fail")
Hint: add the admittances \(1/Z\) of parallel branches, then invert. With the course's values, 10 × 22 µF fails (about 9.7 mΩ) and 12 passes (about 8.5 mΩ). The project uses 14 for about 13 per cent margin.

docs.title: Who this book is for
docs.text:
This book is for undergraduate students and early-career engineers who want to understand random-access memory properly: how a single bit is stored, how billions of bits are arranged on a chip, how the main families of RAM (SRAM, DDR, LPDDR, GDDR, HBM and the non-volatile newcomers) differ and why, and how a real DDR5 memory module is put together from chips, helper chips, copper and firmware. No prior knowledge of memory design is assumed. Terms are explained when they first appear, and a glossary at the end collects them. A first course in digital logic and some comfort with simple arithmetic and units are all that is needed. Readers who know a little circuit theory (resistors, capacitors, the idea of an impedance) will find the chapters on signals and power easier, but each of those chapters starts from first principles.

The book joins two pieces of teaching material that were written for the same audience from different directions. The first is a practical tutorial on RAM types, which surveys every major memory family generation by generation and then looks behind the product at how memory is designed, manufactured and sold. The second is a course called Designing RAM from Scratch, which follows one worked example, a 32 GB DDR5 server memory module, from the single bit up to the files sent to a circuit-board factory, with calculations, small simulations and fourteen graded assignments. Where the two overlap they have been merged into one text. Where the course used interactive demonstrations, the book gives the same calculation as a worked example, a table or a static figure, so that every number can be checked with a pencil.

docs.title: How the book is organised
docs.text:
The chapters run from the bit to the product.

Chapters Subject 1 to 3 What RAM is; how SRAM and DRAM cells store a bit; how a DRAM chip is organised and how a read, a refresh and error correction work 4 to 9 The families: the SRAM family, standard DDR, LPDDR and GDDR, HBM and specialty DRAM, module formats, and the non-volatile memories 10 Choosing among the families, with a comparison table and bandwidth worked examples 11 to 14 A complete worked example, the 32 GB DDR5 registered module: its specification and datasheets, the signals, the power delivery, and the board, firmware, testing and manufacture 15 to 17 Behind the product: how an SRAM is designed, what a process design kit and a process node are, what designing a controller or a DRAM chip involves, the memory market, and what a student can actually build with open-source tools Back matter A glossary and a list of further reading

Each chapter opens with a short statement of what it covers and ends with a summary and exercises. Every exercise has its answer in a folded block: try the exercise first, then open the answer. Worked examples appear in boxes headed "Example", with every step shown.

docs.title: Using the book
docs.text: A reader who only wants to know which memory to choose can read Chapters 1, 3 and 10 and look up the families in between. A reader who wants to understand DDR5 in depth should read Chapters 1 to 3, then 5 and 8, and then the case-study chapters 11 to 14. Anyone interested in memory design as a career will find the practical routes in Chapters 15 to 17, together with the assignments that are placed at the ends of the chapters to which they belong. The assignments are small projects. The early ones need only a calculator or a few lines of Python; the later ones use circuit simulators, a board-design program, a hardware description language or a layout editor, and the last is a capstone to be scoped by the reader.

docs.title: Conventions and cautions
docs.text:
Several habits of the memory industry cause confusion, so they are fixed here.

  • Data rate and clock. Modern memory moves data on both edges of the clock, so a part sold as DDR5-6400 runs a 3200 MHz clock and carries 6400 megatransfers per second (MT/s) on each data pin. The book always says which of the two it means.
  • Bandwidth and capacity units. Bandwidth is quoted in decimal units (1 GB/s is 1000 MB/s). Capacity of DRAM is binary (1 GB is \(2^{30}\) bytes). The chip sizes in gigabits (Gb) are also binary multiples.
  • Newest generations. The details of LPDDR6, HBM4, DDR6 and the fastest GDDR7 speeds were still changing in 2026, when the source material was prepared. Their figures should be read as targets or early values. Standards from JEDEC, the body that writes memory standards, and vendor data sheets are the final authority for any design.
  • Costs, headcounts and market sizes. Where the book gives money or people, the figures are rough orders of magnitude that vary between companies and years, and are meant to give a sense of scale.
  • The worked example. The 32 GB module of Chapters 11 to 14 comes from a student project in which the module was designed as code. Its numbers (currents, impedances, timings) come from the project's calculations and from the manufacturers' data sheets that the project used. They are design-stage figures, not measurements on a built module, and the book says so where it matters. Parts of the project were still unfinished when the material was written; the chapters point out which results are firm and which are open questions.

A last note on tone. The book tries to be honest about what is real and what is only planned. When a statement depends on a vendor's current product, a licence or a price, the chapter says to confirm it with the vendor.

docs.title: Chapter 3: Reading, Writing and the Interface
docs.text: Chapter 2 described what is inside a DRAM chip. This chapter follows the three steps of an access to it (open a row, read a column, close the row), shows why the interface moves data on both clock edges, works through the bandwidth of different speeds and bus widths, explains the multi-level signalling used by the fastest memories, and finishes with error correction, including a small worked code that you can decode by hand. Together these give the vocabulary needed to read a DDR5 data sheet.

docs.title: 3.1 One read, step by step
docs.text:
Reading from DRAM is like using a library: fetch the book, read a line, put the book back. The chip performs three commands.

  1. ACTIVATE (fetch the book). The chip opens one whole row, 8 Kbit per bank in the 16 Gb chip of Chapter 2, into the sense amplifiers, which read the faint charge on each bitline and amplify it. This takes the row-to-column delay \(t_{RCD}\), about 16 ns in the course's DDR5-4800 example.
  2. READ (read a line). The controller picks the column. After the CAS latency (40 clock cycles, about 16.7 ns) the data streams out as a burst of 16 transfers.
  3. PRECHARGE (put the book back). The row is written back into the cells, since reading drained them, and closed, ready for a different row. This takes the precharge time \(t_{RP}\), about 16 ns.

Figure 3.1 draws the timeline for one read to a closed row at DDR5-4800.

Figure 3.1. A timeline with three lanes (commands, row in bank, data pins) showing ACT at 0 ns, READ at 16.25 ns, PRE at 32 ns, a burst of 16 transfers of 3.3 ns starting at 32.9 ns, and braces for tRCD, CL and tRP

The numbers behind the figure come from the clock. DDR5-4800 has a 2400 MHz clock, so one cycle lasts \(1000/2400 = 0.4167\) ns. Then \(t_{RCD} = 39\) cycles \(= 16.25\) ns, \(\text{CL} = 40\) cycles \(= 16.67\) ns, \(t_{RP} = 39\) cycles \(= 16.25\) ns. The burst of 16 transfers at 4800 MT/s lasts \(16 / 4800\ \text{MT/s} = 3.33\) ns.

Example 3.1: Row miss versus row hit

Using the DDR5-4800 numbers above, how long until the first data appears?

  1. Closed row (miss to an idle bank): ACTIVATE, wait \(t_{RCD}\), READ, wait CL: \(16.25 + 16.67 = 32.9\) ns, which is where the burst starts in Figure 3.1.
  2. Open row (hit): the row is already in the sense amplifiers, so only READ and CL remain: 16.7 ns.
  3. Open the wrong row (conflict): the old row must be precharged first, then the new one activated: \(t_{RP} + t_{RCD} + \text{CL} = 16.25 + 16.25 + 16.67 = 49.2\) ns.

That the three cases differ by a factor of three is why memory controllers try to group requests that go to the same row. Bank groups and several banks let the controller open a row in one bank while another bank transfers data, hiding part of the delay.

docs.title: 3.2 Double data rate
docs.text:
A clock is a heartbeat that ticks up and down. Older memory moved one piece of data per tick. DDR (double data rate) moves data on the way up and on the way down, doubling the throughput at the same clock. A single-rate waiter carries plates only into the dining room; a DDR waiter also carries dirty plates back on every return trip, so the same number of trips does twice the work.

The first SDRAM (synchronous DRAM) moved data once per clock cycle. A DDR4-3200 module therefore runs a 1600 MHz clock. The DRAM array inside the chip has stayed at only a few hundred MHz across all generations. To feed an ever-faster interface, each generation fetches more bits per data pin from the array at once, the prefetch, and sends them out in a burst. The prefetch has doubled from 2n (DDR) to 4n (DDR2), 8n (DDR3) and 16n (DDR5). DDR4 kept 8n but added bank groups so that commands to different groups can overlap. Chapter 5 follows this history generation by generation.

docs.title: 3.3 Bandwidth at different speeds and widths
docs.text:
Bandwidth equals the number of transfers per second times the bus width divided by 8. At 4800 MT/s on a 64-bit bus: \(4800 \times 64 / 8 / 1000 = 38.4\) GB/s. Table 3.1 gives peak bandwidth for a range of DDR5 speeds and three bus widths: 32 bits (one DDR5 sub-channel), 64 bits (one DIMM) and 128 bits (two DIMMs). The last two columns give the clock and the duration of one bit on a data pin.

Speed (MT/s) 32-bit (GB/s) 64-bit (GB/s) 128-bit (GB/s) Clock (MHz) One bit lasts (ns) 3200 12.8 25.6 51.2 1600 0.313 4800 19.2 38.4 76.8 2400 0.208 5600 22.4 44.8 89.6 2800 0.179 6400 25.6 51.2 102.4 3200 0.156 8000 32.0 64.0 128.0 4000 0.125 8800 35.2 70.4 140.8 4400 0.114

Table 3.1: Peak bandwidth of DDR5 speeds.

At 4800 MT/s each bit lasts only about 0.2 ns, and in that time a signal travels about 3 cm along a circuit board. That fact motivates Chapter 12: wires at these speeds stop being simple connections.

docs.title: 3.4 Signalling: NRZ, PAM3 and PAM4
docs.text:
Each transfer on a wire is a symbol, sent as a voltage level. Classic NRZ (non-return-to-zero) uses two levels, so each symbol is one bit. To go faster without raising the symbol rate (which makes signals harder to receive cleanly), newer interfaces use more levels. PAM4 (four-level pulse amplitude modulation) carries 2 bits per symbol, and PAM3 carries 3 bits in every 2 symbols, which is 1.5 bits per symbol. More levels mean smaller gaps between the levels, so receivers must be more sensitive and noise matters more. PAM3 balances this trade-off between NRZ and PAM4.

Figure 3.2. Eight symbol slots drawn with NRZ (two levels, one bit per symbol), PAM3 (three levels, three bits per two symbols) and PAM4 (four levels, two bits per symbol), with the memory interfaces that use each

NRZ is used by DDR4 and DDR5, LPDDR and GDDR6. PAM3 is used by GDDR7. PAM4 is used by GDDR6X and by PCIe 6.0.

Example 3.2: Bits per second with multi-level signalling

A GDDR7 pin runs at up to 32 Gbps in first products, counting bits. With PAM3's 1.5 bits per symbol, the symbol rate is \(32 / 1.5 = 21.3\) gigasymbols per second. A PAM4 link carrying the same 32 Gbps would need only \(32/2 = 16\) gigasymbols per second, and NRZ would need 32. The price of fewer symbols is smaller voltage steps: with a fixed total swing, adjacent levels are the whole swing apart in NRZ, half of it apart in PAM3 and one third of it apart in PAM4. PAM3 sits between the two on both counts.

docs.title: 3.5 Error correction: side-band, on-die and inline ECC
docs.text:
Cosmic rays, alpha particles, electrical noise and weak cells occasionally flip a bit. Servers cannot afford that, so they store extra check bits computed from the data. When reading, the check bits reveal which bit flipped, and the controller flips it back. This is ECC (error-correcting code). There are three quite different kinds.

  • Side-band ECC adds extra chips to the module: 72 bits instead of 64 on DDR4, or \(2 \times 40\) bits instead of \(2 \times 32\) on DDR5. The memory controller computes and checks the code, so it protects the whole path, including the wires on the board, and errors can be logged. This is what "ECC memory" means for servers and workstations.
  • On-die ECC (DDR5, LPDDR5 and later) is computed inside each DRAM chip and is invisible to the system. It fixes single-bit errors in the array, which lets vendors keep yields up on dense chips, but it does not protect the bus and does not replace side-band ECC.
  • Inline ECC, used in some LPDDR systems, stores check bits in a reserved part of normal memory instead of extra chips, at some cost in capacity and bandwidth.

The 32 GB module of Chapters 11 to 14 stores 8 check bits for every 32 data bits (a 40-bit sub-channel), which is why it has 20 memory chips instead of 16.

docs.title: A worked code: Hamming(7,4)
docs.text:
Real server ECC uses larger codes, but the idea is the same as in the classic Hamming(7,4) code: 4 data bits \(d_1 \dots d_4\) plus 3 check bits \(p_1, p_2, p_3\), placed in seven positions:

position:  1   2   3   4   5   6   7
bit:       p1  p2  d1  p3  d2  d3  d4

The check bits are parities (exclusive-ORs): \(p_1 = d_1 \oplus d_2 \oplus d_4\), \(p_2 = d_1 \oplus d_3 \oplus d_4\), \(p_3 = d_2 \oplus d_3 \oplus d_4\). On reading, three syndrome bits are recomputed over the stored word: \(s_1 = c_1 \oplus c_3 \oplus c_5 \oplus c_7\), \(s_2 = c_2 \oplus c_3 \oplus c_6 \oplus c_7\), \(s_3 = c_4 \oplus c_5 \oplus c_6 \oplus c_7\). The number \(s_1 + 2 s_2 + 4 s_3\) is the position of the flipped bit, or 0 if there is no error.

Example 3.3: Break a bit, watch it get fixed

Store the data \(d_1 d_2 d_3 d_4 = 1\,0\,1\,1\).

  1. Check bits: \(p_1 = 1 \oplus 0 \oplus 1 = 0\), \(p_2 = 1 \oplus 1 \oplus 1 = 1\), \(p_3 = 0 \oplus 1 \oplus 1 = 0\).
  2. The stored codeword (positions 1 to 7) is 0 1 1 0 0 1 1.
  3. A cosmic ray flips position 6, so the memory returns 0 1 1 0 0 0 1.
  4. Syndrome: \(s_1 = 0 \oplus 1 \oplus 0 \oplus 1 = 0\); \(s_2 = 1 \oplus 1 \oplus 0 \oplus 1 = 1\); \(s_3 = 0 \oplus 0 \oplus 0 \oplus 1 = 1\).
  5. \(s_1 + 2 s_2 + 4 s_3 = 0 + 2 + 4 = 6\): position 6 is wrong. Flip it back and read the data bits from positions 3, 5, 6, 7: 1 0 1 1, the original.

A single-error code

Hamming(7,4) corrects one flipped bit. With two flipped bits it points at the wrong position and silently produces wrong data. Server ECC adds bits so that it can at least detect two errors.

docs.title: 3.6 Summary
docs.text:
• A read is three commands: ACTIVATE (open a row into the sense amplifiers), READ (select a column; data appears after CAS latency as a burst) and PRECHARGE (write the row back and close it).
  • For DDR5-4800, \(t_{RCD}\) is 16.25 ns, CL is 16.7 ns, \(t_{RP}\) is 16.25 ns and a burst of 16 lasts 3.3 ns. Hits to an open row are three times quicker than conflicts.
  • DDR moves data on both clock edges; prefetch lets a slow array feed a fast interface.
  • NRZ carries 1 bit per symbol, PAM3 1.5 and PAM4 2.
  • Side-band ECC protects the whole path; on-die ECC protects only the array; inline ECC borrows ordinary memory. Hamming codes locate a flipped bit by a syndrome.

docs.title: 3.7 Exercises
docs.text:
Exercise 3.1. For DDR5-6400 (3200 MHz clock) with \(t_{RCD} = 46\) cycles, CL = 46 cycles and \(t_{RP} = 46\) cycles, find the clock period and the times for a row hit, a row miss on an idle bank and a row conflict.

Answer

The clock period is \(1000/3200 = 0.3125\) ns, so each of the three parameters is \(46 \times 0.3125 = 14.375\) ns. Row hit: 14.4 ns. Miss on an idle bank: \(14.375 + 14.375 = 28.75\) ns. Conflict: \(3 \times 14.375 = 43.1\) ns.

Exercise 3.2. One DDR5 sub-channel has 32 data pins and a burst length of 16. How many bytes does one burst carry, and how long does the burst last at 4800 MT/s?

Answer

\(16 \times 32 / 8 = 64\) bytes, one cache line. At 4800 MT/s the 16 transfers last \(16/4800\,\text{MT/s} = 3.33\) ns.

Exercise 3.3. Encode the data 0 1 1 0 in Hamming(7,4), flip position 3 of the codeword and decode it.

Answer

\(d_1 d_2 d_3 d_4 = 0\,1\,1\,0\). \(p_1 = 0 \oplus 1 \oplus 0 = 1\), \(p_2 = 0 \oplus 1 \oplus 0 = 1\), \(p_3 = 1 \oplus 1 \oplus 0 = 0\). Codeword (positions 1 to 7): \(p_1 p_2 d_1 p_3 d_2 d_3 d_4 = 1\,1\,0\,0\,1\,1\,0\). Flipping position 3 gives 1 1 1 0 1 1 0. Syndrome: \(s_1 = c_1 \oplus c_3 \oplus c_5 \oplus c_7 = 1 \oplus 1 \oplus 1 \oplus 0 = 1\); \(s_2 = c_2 \oplus c_3 \oplus c_6 \oplus c_7 = 1 \oplus 1 \oplus 1 \oplus 0 = 1\); \(s_3 = c_4 \oplus c_5 \oplus c_6 \oplus c_7 = 0 \oplus 1 \oplus 1 \oplus 0 = 0\). The syndrome is \(1 + 2 + 0 = 3\), so position 3 is flipped back, and the data bits at positions 3, 5, 6, 7 are 0 1 1 0.

Exercise 3.4. A memory interface must carry 24 Gbps per pin. How many symbols per second per pin does it need with NRZ, PAM3 and PAM4?

Answer

NRZ (1 bit per symbol): 24 Gsymbols/s. PAM3 (1.5 bits per symbol): \(24/1.5 = 16\) Gsymbols/s. PAM4 (2 bits per symbol): 12 Gsymbols/s. The fewer symbols per second, the easier the timing, but the smaller the voltage gaps between levels.

Exercise 3.5 (Assignment 12: a tiny memory controller). Write a Verilog state machine that issues ACTIVATE, then READ, then PRECHARGE with counters for \(t_{RCD}\), CL and \(t_{RP}\) in clock cycles. Write a cocotb behavioural DRAM model that raises an error if any timing is violated. Run reads to random rows and columns, then deliberately shorten \(t_{RCD}\) by one cycle.

Answer

At DDR5-4800 the clock is 2400 MHz, so \(t_{RCD}\) of 16.25 ns is 39 cycles. A simple controller (precharge timing simplified, since a real DRAM also enforces a minimum row-open time and write recovery) is:

module memctl #(parameter TRCD = 39, CL = 40, TRP = 39) (
    input  wire clk, rst, req,
    output reg  act, rd, pre, data_valid, busy
);
    localparam IDLE = 0, RCD = 1, CAS = 2, RP = 3;
    reg [1:0] state;
    reg [7:0] cnt;
    always @(posedge clk) begin
        act <= 0; rd <= 0; pre <= 0; data_valid <= 0;
        if (rst) begin state <= IDLE; busy <= 0; cnt <= 0; end
        else case (state)
            IDLE: if (req) begin
                      act <= 1; busy <= 1; cnt <= TRCD - 1; state <= RCD;
                  end
            RCD:  if (cnt == 0) begin rd <= 1; cnt <= CL - 1; state <= CAS; end
                  else cnt <= cnt - 1;
            CAS:  if (cnt == 0) begin
                      data_valid <= 1; pre <= 1; cnt <= TRP - 1; state <= RP;
                  end else cnt <= cnt - 1;
            RP:   if (cnt == 0) begin busy <= 0; state <= IDLE; end
                  else cnt <= cnt - 1;
        endcase
    end
endmodule

The cocotb model records the cycle of each command and asserts that READ comes at least \(t_{RCD}\) cycles after ACTIVATE and the next ACTIVATE at least \(t_{RP}\) after PRECHARGE. Expected result: all reads pass with the correct timings, and the version with \(t_{RCD}\) shortened by one cycle must make the model report a violation.

docs.title: Chapter 12: Signals: When a Wire Stops Being Just a Wire
docs.text: At 4800 million transfers per second, each bit lasts about 0.2 nanoseconds. In that time a signal travels only about 3 cm along the board. Wires start to behave like water pipes that echo. This chapter explains why, using the 32 GB module of Chapter 11 as the example: the characteristic impedance of a trace, the echoes that a mismatched end produces, the eye diagram that engineers use to judge whether a link will work, and the fly-by command bus that visits five chips in a row and the study that chose its termination.

docs.title: 12.1 Why wires behave differently at speed
docs.text: At 4800 MT/s one bit lasts \(1000/4800 = 0.208\) ns. A signal on a printed circuit board moves at roughly half the speed of light, about 15 cm per nanosecond, so in one bit time it covers about 3 cm. The DRAM package of this project is 7.5 × 11 mm, so a bit is only a few chip-widths long, and shorter than many of the wires carrying it. When wires are long compared with the signal's rise time, you can no longer treat a wire as one electrical point. The signal travels along it as a wave, and what happens at the far end matters.

docs.title: 12.2 Impedance and echoes
docs.text:
Every fast wire has a characteristic impedance \(Z_0\): how hard it "pushes back" on a signal. The traces of the module are designed at 40 Ω by choosing the trace width and the distance to the copper plane underneath. If the end of the wire does not match \(Z_0\), part of the signal reflects. The fraction is the reflection coefficient

\[\Gamma = \frac{R - Z_0}{R + Z_0},\]

where \(R\) is the resistance at the end. A termination resistor equal to \(Z_0\) absorbs the signal completely, with no echo.

Flick a rope tied to a wall and the wave bounces back. Tie it to an identical rope that runs on forever and the wave just keeps going. A matched termination is the "rope that runs on forever".

Example 12.1: Echoes from different line ends

The line has \(Z_0 = 40\ \Omega\). Evaluate \(\Gamma\) for five line ends.

End R \(\Gamma = (R-40)/(R+40)\) What happens Short circuit 0 Ω \(-40/40 = -1\) Echo of full size, inverted 20 Ω resistor 20 Ω \(-20/60 = -0.33\) Echo a third of the size, inverted Matched 40 Ω \(0\) No echo 80 Ω resistor 80 Ω \(40/120 = +0.33\) Echo a third of the size, same polarity Open end very large \(\to +1\) Echo of full size, same polarity

A 1 V step sent into the 20 Ω end therefore returns a 0.33 V echo of opposite sign; into the open end it returns 1 V of the same sign, which adds to the incoming step and can overshoot the voltage limit of the receiver.

Figure 12.1. Reflection coefficient against end resistor for a 40 ohm line, falling to minus one at 0 ohms, zero at 40 ohms and rising towards plus one for large resistances

docs.title: 12.3 The eye diagram
docs.text:
Take a long random stream of bits, cut it into two-bit slices and draw all the slices on top of each other. The empty diamond in the middle is the eye. The receiver decides 0 or 1 in the middle of it, so it needs the eye to be tall (voltage margin) and wide (timing margin).

Three effects close the eye:

  • Faster signalling gives less time per bit, so the wire's slowness smears one bit into the next.
  • Echoes from mismatched ends add ghost copies of the signal.
  • Noise blurs everything.

The course's demonstration made this visible with a simple model: a pseudo-random bit sequence (PRBS7, which repeats every 127 bits) passed through a first-order low-pass filter with a time constant of 0.06 ns, plus a single echo 0.27 ns later and Gaussian noise. A mask of 0.3 V in height and 0.4 bit in width, centred in the eye, decides pass or fail. Figure 12.2 recreates it at three speeds with a 10 per cent echo and 12 mV of noise.

Figure 12.2. Three eye diagrams at 3200, 4800 and 9600 MT/s, with measured eye heights of 783, 699 and 461 mV and widths of 0.97, 0.93 and 0.72 bit, the dashed mask in the middle of each

The eye shrinks steadily with speed: from 783 mV high and 0.97 bit wide at 3200 MT/s to 461 mV and 0.72 bit at 9600 MT/s. All three pass the mask of this simple model, but the margin at 9600 is far thinner, and real channels add more impairments than this toy model.

The real project eye is shown in Figure 12.3: the module's data path simulated in ngspice for a write to the top DRAM at 4800 MT/s with on-die termination of 60 Ω. The eye is wide open.

Figure 12.3. Simulated DDR5-4800 write eye diagram from ngspice for the module's data path, with voltage at the receiver between 0.5 V and 1.1 V, and a reference level at 0.8 V

What the reference level does

The dashed line in Figure 12.3 is \(V_{ref}\), 0.800 V, the level the receiver compares the incoming signal against to decide 0 or 1. The signal swings between about 0.5 V and 1.1 V, so the reference sits near the middle of the eye, which is where the crossing points of the traces lie.

docs.title: 12.4 The command bus: a fly-by with five stops
docs.text:
Data wires run point to point, one wire to one chip. But each command must reach many chips. The RCD drives one long wire that visits five chips like bus stops. This is the fly-by topology of Section 5.5. Each stop adds load and an echo, and the signal reaches the last chip later than the first. The chips cope with the arrival delay through a calibration called write levelling. The echoes must be tamed by choosing the wire impedance, the driver strength and the termination.

The course's demonstration used a simple model of this: a loaded line. Every chip adds capacitance, which lowers the effective impedance of the wire, and slows the signal. With a signal delay of 6.62 ps per millimetre of unloaded wire, 0.132 pF of wire capacitance per millimetre, 1.33 pF per chip and a first chip 15 mm from the RCD, the slowing factor is \(k = \sqrt{1 + C_{load}/(C' \cdot p)}\) for chip pitch \(p\), the loaded impedance is \(50/k\) ohms, and the arrival time at chip \(i\) (counting from 0) is \((15 + i\,p)\times 6.62 \times k\) ps.

Example 12.2: Fly-by arrival times

  1. Pitch 11.5 mm (the project's chip spacing): \(C'p = 0.132 \times 11.5 = 1.518\) pF, so \(k = \sqrt{1 + 1.33/1.518} = 1.37\). Loaded impedance \(= 50/1.37 = 36.5\ \Omega\).
  2. Arrival times: chip 0 at \(15 \times 6.62 \times 1.37 = 136\) ps; then 240, 345, 449 and 553 ps for chips 1 to 4.
  3. The last chip hears the command \(553 - 136 = 417\) ps after the first. That is nearly two bit times at 4800 MT/s (0.208 ns), which is why write levelling is needed.
Pitch (mm) \(k\) Loaded impedance (Ω) First chip (ps) Last chip (ps) Spread (ps) 8.0 1.50 33.3 149 468 318 11.5 1.37 36.5 136 553 417 16.0 1.28 39.2 127 668 541

Wider spacing lowers the loading (the impedance rises towards 50 Ω) but makes the spread larger.

The project simulated 48 combinations of wire impedance, driver strength and termination (and 27 alternative ones). Ten passed. The chosen combination is a 50 Ω wire, a 20 Ω driver and a 48 Ω termination inside the last chip. The result: an eye about 0.6 bit wide, with an overshoot of 227 mV against a limit of 250 mV. That margin is thin, which is an honest thing to note: the design passes, but with little to spare.

Figure 12.4. Simulated command-and-address eye at the last DRAM of the fly-by, at 2400 Mb/s, with a 50 ohm wire, a 20 ohm driver and a 48 ohm pod termination, reference level 0.743 V

docs.title: 12.5 Summary
docs.text:
• At 4800 MT/s a bit lasts 0.208 ns and a signal moves about 3 cm in that time, so wires behave as transmission lines with a characteristic impedance (40 Ω for the module's traces).
  • A mismatch reflects \(\Gamma = (R - Z_0)/(R + Z_0)\) of the signal; a termination equal to \(Z_0\) removes the echo.
  • The eye diagram shows voltage and timing margin; speed, echoes and noise all close it.
  • The command bus is a fly-by that loads the wire, delays the signal differently at each chip (write levelling compensates) and needs a termination chosen by simulation. The project chose a 50 Ω wire, 20 Ω driver and 48 Ω termination, with thin margins.

docs.title: 12.6 Exercises
docs.text:
Exercise 12.1. A 40 Ω line ends in a 60 Ω resistor. Find \(\Gamma\) and the size and sign of the echo for a 1.1 V step.

Answer

\(\Gamma = (60-40)/(60+40) = 0.2\). The echo is \(+0.22\) V, the same polarity as the step.

Exercise 12.2. How far does a signal travel in one bit time at 6400 MT/s, if it moves at 15 cm per nanosecond?

Answer

One bit lasts \(1000/6400 = 0.156\) ns, so the signal travels \(0.156 \times 15 = 2.3\) cm.

Exercise 12.3. At 4800 MT/s the fly-by spread is 417 ps with 11.5 mm spacing. Express this in bit times of the data signal and in clock cycles of the 2400 MHz clock.

Answer

A bit lasts 208 ps, so \(417/208 \approx 2.0\) bit times. A clock cycle lasts 417 ps, so the spread is almost exactly one clock cycle. Write levelling aligns the data to each chip's clock arrival.

Exercise 12.4 (Assignment 7: find the best termination). In ngspice, drive a 40 Ω, 100 ps line (a T element) from a 34 Ω driver and end it in a resistor \(R\). Sweep \(R\) from 20 to 200 Ω and record the overshoot and ringing at the end. Add five 1 pF loads along the line (a fly-by) and repeat. Plot overshoot against \(R\) for both.

Answer

The best \(R\) is about 40 Ω for the plain line, and the measured echo matches \(\Gamma = (R-40)/(R+40)\). With five loads the best \(R\) falls, to around 30 Ω in the course's check, because the loaded impedance is lower than \(Z_0\). The hint is \(Z_{loaded} \approx Z_0 / \sqrt{1 + C_{load}/C_{segment}}\). The exact value depends on how the loads are spaced along the line, so take the number from your own sweep and confirm it lies below 40 Ω.

Exercise 12.5 (Assignment 8: build an eye diagram from scratch). In Python with NumPy, generate PRBS7 bits with a 7-bit shift register (taps 7 and 6), pass the waveform through a first-order low-pass filter (time constant \(\tau\)), add Gaussian noise, cut it into 2-bit slices, overlay them and measure the eye height and width. Sweep the data rate.

Answer 

import numpy as np

def prbs7(n):
    reg, out = 0x7F, []
    for _ in range(n):
        new = ((reg >> 6) ^ (reg >> 5)) & 1      # taps 7 and 6
        reg = ((reg << 1) | new) & 0x7F
        out.append(new)
    return np.array(out)

def eye_height(mts, tau_ns=0.06, noise=0.012, spu=40, nbits=508):
    bits = prbs7(nbits)
    dt = (1000.0 / mts) / spu                    # ns per sample
    a = 1 - np.exp(-dt / tau_ns)
    x = np.repeat(bits, spu).astype(float)
    y, s = np.zeros_like(x), 0.0
    for i, v in enumerate(x):
        s += a * (v - s); y[i] = s               # first-order low-pass
    y += noise * np.random.default_rng(1).standard_normal(len(y))
    idx = np.arange(10, nbits - 10) * spu + spu // 2 + int(0.7 * tau_ns / dt)
    sent = bits[idx // spu]
    return y[idx][sent == 1].min() - y[idx][sent == 0].max()
Check: PRBS7 repeats every 127 bits (prbs7(254) has two equal halves). With \(\tau = 0.06\) ns and 12 mV of noise (no echo), this code gives eye heights of about 0.94 V at 1600 MT/s, 0.87 V at 3200, 0.78 V at 4800, 0.67 V at 6400 and 0.54 V at 9600, where one bit lasts only 1.7 \(\tau\). The eye closes faster still once echoes are added, and the course's check is that it closes sharply once one bit lasts only about 2 to 3 \(\tau\). Measure the height at the centre of the bit, using the known transmitted bits to separate ones from zeros.

docs.title: Chapter 5: Standard DDR SDRAM: From SDR to DDR6
docs.text: DDR SDRAM is the main memory of personal computers and servers. It is optimised for the lowest cost per bit and for large capacities, with modules that plug into slots. This chapter follows the family generation by generation, from the first synchronous DRAM of 1993 to DDR5 and the DDR6 that is in development, and shows what changed each time: the prefetch, the voltage, the topology, the error handling. It then looks closely at what made DDR5 the largest architectural change in the series.

docs.title: 5.1 What "double data rate" means
docs.text:
SDRAM (synchronous DRAM) is DRAM whose interface follows a clock. The first SDRAM moved data once per clock cycle. Double data rate SDRAM moves data on both the rising and the falling edge, doubling throughput without doubling the clock. A DDR4-3200 module therefore runs a 1600 MHz clock.

Inside the chip, the DRAM array has stayed at only a few hundred MHz across all generations. The interface speeds up by fetching more bits per data pin from the array at once, and the prefetch has doubled from 2n (DDR) to 4n (DDR2), 8n (DDR3) and 16n (DDR5). DDR4 kept 8n and added bank groups.

Example 5.1: How fast does the array really run?

Divide the data rate by the prefetch to get the rate at which the array is accessed.

Generation Data rate (MT/s) Prefetch Array access rate DDR-400 400 2n 200 MHz DDR2-800 800 4n 200 MHz DDR3-1600 1600 8n 200 MHz DDR4-3200 3200 8n 400 MHz DDR5-6400 6400 16n 400 MHz

Across a factor of 16 in data rate, the array access rate has only doubled. DDR4 kept the 8n prefetch and so had to speed up the array itself, but it eased the burden with bank groups, which let commands to different groups overlap.

DDR5 made the biggest architectural changes of the family:

  • Two independent 32-bit sub-channels per DIMM instead of one 64-bit channel, so more requests can run in parallel.
  • An on-DIMM PMIC (power-management IC): voltage regulation moved from the motherboard onto the module, giving cleaner power at 1.1 V.
  • On-die ECC inside every chip, to keep dense chips reliable.
  • Same-bank refresh, which refreshes one bank in each bank group while the others keep working, instead of stalling the whole chip.
  • Burst length 16, up to 32 banks in 8 bank groups, and receiver equalisation to handle the higher speeds.

DDR6 is in development at JEDEC, the industry body that writes memory standards (Section 5.8).

docs.title: 5.2 SDR SDRAM (1993)
docs.text: Single data rate SDRAM replaced the asynchronous FPM and EDO DRAM of the early 1990s (Chapter 7). Synchronising to the system bus clock let the controller pipeline commands, and multiple internal banks let one bank open a row while another transferred data. PC66, PC100 and PC133 modules ran at 66 to 133 MHz on a 3.3 V supply, giving about 1 GB/s on a 64-bit bus. SDR SDRAM powered the Pentium II and Pentium III era and is now obsolete outside some very old industrial equipment.

docs.title: 5.3 DDR (2000)
docs.text: The first DDR generation transferred data on both clock edges using a 2n prefetch, giving 200 to 400 MT/s at 2.5 V and up to 3.2 GB/s per 64-bit channel. It introduced a data strobe signal (DQS) that travels with the data, so that the receiver knows exactly when to sample it. DDR used 184-pin DIMMs and was the mainstream memory for Athlon XP and Pentium 4 PCs. It is obsolete.

docs.title: 5.4 DDR2 (2003)
docs.text: DDR2 doubled the prefetch to 4n, so the interface could run twice as fast as the array: 400 to 1066 MT/s at 1.8 V, up to about 8.5 GB/s per channel. It added on-die termination (ODT), resistors inside the chip that absorb signal reflections and so improve signal quality on busy buses (Chapter 12). Latency in cycles went up, but latency in nanoseconds stayed similar. DDR2 used 240-pin DIMMs and is obsolete.

docs.title: 5.5 DDR3 and DDR3L (2007)
docs.text: DDR3 moved to an 8n prefetch and 800 to 2133 MT/s at 1.5 V; the low-voltage DDR3L version runs at 1.35 V. Peak bandwidth reached about 17 GB/s per channel. DDR3 introduced the fly-by topology, where command and address signals pass each chip on the module in turn, with write levelling to compensate for the different arrival times (Section 12.4). DDR3 had a long life, and DDR3L is still found in some embedded boards and industrial systems.

docs.title: 5.6 DDR4 (2014)
docs.text: DDR4 kept the 8n prefetch but organised banks into bank groups (typically 4 groups of 4 banks), allowing faster back-to-back access to different groups. It ran at 1600 to 3200 MT/s in the JEDEC standard (enthusiast modules went higher) at 1.2 V, giving 25.6 GB/s per channel at 3200 MT/s. Other additions were pseudo-open-drain I/O to save power, data bus inversion and CRC error detection on writes. DDR4 served the PC and server world for most of a decade and is now being phased out in favour of DDR5.

docs.title: 5.7 DDR5 (2020)
docs.text:
DDR5 is the current mainstream generation. Standard speeds started at 4800 MT/s, and the JEDEC standard now extends to 8800 MT/s at 1.1 V. That gives 38.4 GB/s per 64-bit DIMM at 4800 MT/s and 70.4 GB/s at 8800 MT/s. Each DIMM carries two 32-bit sub-channels, its own PMIC, and chips with on-die ECC and same-bank refresh. Chip capacity grew to 16, 24 and 32 Gbit, so single modules of 48 GB, 64 GB and far larger server modules are common. At the highest speeds desktop modules add a clock driver chip (the CUDIMM), and servers can use MRDIMMs; see Chapter 8.

Example 5.2: From chip capacity to module capacity

A DDR5 DIMM has two 32-bit sub-channels, 64 data bits in all. With x8 chips (8 data pins each), \(64/8 = 8\) chips fill one rank.

  1. With 16 Gb chips: \(8 \times 16 = 128\) Gb \(= 16\) GB per rank.
  2. With 24 Gb chips: \(8 \times 24 = 192\) Gb \(= 24\) GB per rank. Two ranks give the 48 GB modules mentioned above.
  3. With 32 Gb chips: one rank is 32 GB, and two ranks 64 GB.

An ECC module adds check bits: \(2 \times (32 + 8) = 80\) bits per rank, which is 10 x8 chips or 20 x4 chips (Chapter 11).

A correction to a common figure

Some summaries quote DDR5 as "51 to 70 GB/s per DIMM". That range corresponds to 6400 to 8800 MT/s. DDR5 starts at 4800 MT/s, which is 38.4 GB/s (\(4800 \times 64 / 8 / 1000\)), so the whole standard range is 38 to 70 GB/s per DIMM.

docs.title: 5.8 DDR6 (in development)
docs.text: JEDEC is developing DDR6, with first products expected around 2027 or later. Early public reports suggest data rates starting near 8800 MT/s and aiming towards roughly 17,600 MT/s, about twice the bandwidth of DDR5, with narrower sub-channels to keep efficiency high and a likely shift to new module formats such as CAMM-style connectors at the higher speeds. All details were still subject to change in 2026.

docs.title: 5.9 DDR generations at a glance
docs.text:
Generation Year Speed (MT/s) Voltage Prefetch Bandwidth per 64-bit channel Status SDR SDRAM 1993 66–133 3.3 V 1n ~1 GB/s Obsolete DDR 2000 200–400 2.5 V 2n 3.2 GB/s Obsolete DDR2 2003 400–1066 1.8 V 4n 8.5 GB/s Obsolete DDR3/DDR3L 2007 800–2133 1.5 / 1.35 V 8n 17 GB/s Legacy / embedded DDR4 2014 1600–3200 1.2 V 8n 25.6 GB/s Being phased out DDR5 2020 4800–8800 1.1 V 16n 38–70 GB/s Current mainstream DDR6 ~2027+ target ~8800–17,600 lower not stated ~2× DDR5 In development

Example 5.3: Checking the table

The bandwidth column follows from the top speed of each generation and a 64-bit bus: DDR \(400 \times 8 = 3200\) MB/s; DDR2 \(1066 \times 8 \approx 8.5\) GB/s; DDR3 \(2133 \times 8 \approx 17\) GB/s; DDR4 \(3200 \times 8 = 25.6\) GB/s; DDR5 \(4800 \times 8 = 38.4\) GB/s up to \(8800 \times 8 = 70.4\) GB/s. Each generation roughly doubled peak bandwidth, while the latency in nanoseconds stayed near 10 to 17 ns (Example 1.3).

docs.title: 5.10 Summary
docs.text:
• DDR moves data on both clock edges; the array runs at a few hundred MHz while the interface runs at thousands of MT/s, thanks to prefetch (2n, 4n, 8n, 16n).
  • Each generation added a feature: DQS (DDR), on-die termination (DDR2), fly-by and write levelling (DDR3), bank groups (DDR4), sub-channels, PMIC on the module, on-die ECC and same-bank refresh (DDR5).
  • DDR5 runs at 1.1 V from 4800 to 8800 MT/s; 16, 24 and 32 Gbit chips give 16 to 64 GB modules and far larger server modules.
  • DDR6 was still being defined in 2026.

docs.title: 5.11 Exercises
docs.text:
Exercise 5.1. A DDR3-1866 module has a 64-bit bus. Find its clock frequency, its peak bandwidth and the array access rate (8n prefetch).

Answer

Clock \(= 1866/2 = 933\) MHz. Bandwidth \(= 1866 \times 64 / 8 / 1000 = 14.9\) GB/s. Array access rate \(= 1866/8 = 233\) MHz.

Exercise 5.2. Which generation introduced each: (a) bank groups; (b) on-die termination; (c) the data strobe; (d) the on-module PMIC; (e) fly-by topology?

Answer

(a) DDR4. (b) DDR2. (c) DDR (the first generation). (d) DDR5. (e) DDR3.

Exercise 5.3. A DDR5 ECC RDIMM uses x4 chips of 16 Gb. How many chips are on one rank, and how much is data capacity and raw capacity?

Answer

Bits per rank: \(2 \times (32 + 8) = 80\). With x4 chips: \(80/4 = 20\) chips. Raw: \(20 \times 16 = 320\) Gb \(= 40\) GB. Data: 16 of the 20 chips, \(16 \times 16 = 256\) Gb \(= 32\) GB.

Exercise 5.4. A DDR5 desktop module is sold as DDR5-6000 CL30. Another is DDR5-7200 CL36. Which has the lower CAS latency in nanoseconds?

Answer

DDR5-6000 CL30: \(30 \times 2000/6000 = 10.0\) ns. DDR5-7200 CL36: \(36 \times 2000/7200 = 10.0\) ns. They are equal; the faster module gives more bandwidth at the same latency.

Exercise 5.5. DDR5's burst length is 16 on a 32-bit sub-channel. Explain why a DIMM can serve two cache-line requests at once but a DDR4 DIMM could not.

Answer

Each DDR5 sub-channel has its own command and data wires and delivers \(16 \times 32 / 8 = 64\) bytes, one cache line, per burst, so two sub-channels can serve two requests independently. A DDR4 DIMM is a single 64-bit channel with a burst of 8: it delivers one cache line per burst over the whole width, so a second request has to wait.

docs.title: Chapter 17: The Market, and What You Can Build with Open Tools
docs.text: The last chapter of the main text turns from how memory works to where it is sold and what a student or a small company can realistically do. It first sketches the memory market and the companies in it. It then asks the question every student asks, "could I design a 4 GB RAM with free tools?", and answers it with arithmetic: not as a chip, but yes as a module and as a memory system. It describes the most useful open-source project that can really be manufactured, the role a systems partner can play, and finishes with the toolbox, three career paths and a capstone assignment. Figures for market size and cost are rough orders of magnitude for 2025 and 2026.

docs.title: 17.1 The memory market
docs.text:
Memory is one of the largest and most cyclical parts of the semiconductor industry: prices swing sharply with supply and demand, and AI has reshaped it since 2023. Check current numbers with analysts such as TrendForce, Yole Group or Gartner.

Market Approx. size Notes DRAM (all types) ~USD 130 billion or more (2025), higher in 2026 The biggest semiconductor memory market; surged with AI NAND flash (for comparison) ~USD 65–80 billion Storage rather than RAM Standalone SRAM Under USD 1 billion Most SRAM is embedded inside other chips Emerging NVM (MRAM, FeRAM, ReRAM) ~USD 1–2 billion Small but growing

DRAM revenue by type.

Rank Type Approx. share of DRAM revenue Trend 1 DDR4 / DDR5 (PC and server DIMMs) ~40% Steady; server DDR5 strong 2 LPDDR ~25–30% Spreading into laptops and servers (SOCAMM) 3 HBM ~20–30% and rising fast Fastest growing, highest profit per bit, sold out years ahead 4 GDDR ~5% Graphics and some AI inference 5 Others Small Declining

DRAM revenue by application. Data centres and AI servers (DDR5 RDIMMs, HBM and LPDDR5X) are the biggest and fastest-growing segment, now more than half of DRAM revenue. Smartphones are second by revenue and the largest by number of units. PCs and laptops are third. Graphics, game consoles, automotive and industrial are smaller; automotive is growing as cars gain driver assistance and larger screens.

Who makes DRAM. SK hynix has been number 1 in DRAM revenue since 2025, driven by its lead in HBM. Samsung is a close number 1 or 2 and the largest memory maker overall. Micron is number 3, strong in HBM3E and LPDDR5X. CXMT of China is rising quickly in DDR5 and LPDDR5.

Standard DDR is still the largest type by revenue, LPDDR ships in the most devices, and HBM is the fastest-growing and most profitable. Data-centre memory is where most of the money is going.

docs.title: 17.2 The best open-source route to real RAM silicon
docs.text:
If you can use only open-source tools and open processes, what is the most useful RAM project that can actually be manufactured and that industry will value? The recommendation is to design a custom SRAM macro test chip on an open PDK and, in parallel, build an FPGA-based DDR/LPDDR controller project, which needs no fab at all. Together they exercise the circuit, layout, test and RTL skills that memory teams hire for.

Option Fabricable with open tools? Industry relevant? Verdict DRAM chip No: no open DRAM process exists Yes Not possible LPDDR6 PHY No: 130–180 nm open processes cannot reach 10+ Gbps Yes Not possible in silicon Custom SRAM macro Yes: SKY130, GF180MCU, IHP SG13G2 Yes: every chip has SRAM Best choice DDR/LPDDR controller RTL on FPGA Yes: no fab needed Yes: controller and verification jobs are plentiful Best companion Compute-in-memory SRAM Yes Yes: a hot topic for AI Good stretch goal

Choosing an open PDK. A sensible pick is to learn on SKY130, where the tutorials are, then fabricate on GF180MCU or IHP SG13G2, depending on which affordable shuttle is nearest in time.

PDK Node SRAM support Fabrication route Best for SKY130 130 nm, 1.8 V OpenRAM most mature; most tutorials Shuttle services (Efabless shut down in 2025; check current SKY130 providers) Learning GF180MCU 180 nm, 3.3 / 5 V OpenRAM supported Low-cost pooled runs such as wafer.space; Tiny Tapeout Cheapest real fabrication IHP SG13G2 130 nm SiGe BiCMOS, 1.2 V core Ready-made SRAM macros in the PDK; OpenRAM support in progress IHP open-source MPW runs (sometimes free for open designs), Europractice, Tiny Tapeout Best-quality fab; active European ecosystem

Fabrication access changes often, so always check current schedules and prices. The cheapest possible first silicon is a small test structure on Tiny Tapeout, at a few hundred dollars per tile.

What to put on the test chip. A good test chip is designed for measurement: every block should answer a question about how the SRAM really behaves in silicon.

Block Why include it Custom 1–4 KB 6T single-port SRAM macro The core skill: your own bitcell, periphery and layout OpenRAM macro of the same size A baseline to compare against MBIST (March C− algorithm) Every industry SRAM has built-in self-test Programmable sense-amplifier timing Measure timing margins on real silicon Separate SRAM supply pin Measure Vmin, the lowest voltage at which the SRAM still works Ring oscillators Identify which process corner your chips came from Standalone bitcell and sense-amp test structures Measure static noise margin and sense-amp offset directly SPI or scan test interface Easy to drive from a microcontroller or FPGA Stretch: 8T low-voltage cell or compute-in-memory array Material for a research publication

The open tools for every stage are those of Section 15.3, with KiCad for the test PCB, Python for the measurement analysis, and Git with GitHub Actions running automated DRC, LVS and simulations as regression and CI.

The FPGA companion project. Study LiteDRAM to see how a real open controller and PHY are organised. Use a Lattice ECP5 board with DDR3 memory (for example ButterStick or OrangeCrab) with the open Yosys and nextpnr FPGA flow. Build a simplified DDR3 or LPDDR4-style controller with a scheduler and refresh, verified with a cocotb testbench. Use Ramulator 2.0 or DRAMSim3 to compare scheduling policies. The FPGA board can then serve as the tester for the SRAM chip when it returns from the fab.

Phase Duration Work 0 Ramp-up 1–2 months Install tools, simulate 6T SNM, run OpenRAM 1 Circuit design 3–4 months Bitcell, periphery, timing; corners and Monte Carlo 2 Layout and verification 2–3 months DRC/LVS, extraction, post-layout corners, BIST RTL, test interface 3 Tapeout 1 month Integration, final checks, submission 4 While in fab 3–6 months KiCad test PCB, FPGA tester firmware, controller project 5 Silicon measurement 2–3 months Functional test, shmoo plots, Vmin, access time, leakage, correlation with simulation 6 Publish – GitHub release; conference papers (for example VLSI Design or VDAT in India)

From skills to jobs.

Skill shown by the project Matching job Bitcell and periphery design, Monte Carlo, Vmin Memory circuit design engineer (Intel, AMD, Qualcomm, Arm, Synopsys and Cadence memory-compiler teams) Layout, DRC/LVS, extraction Custom / memory layout engineer .lib characterisation Library / characterisation engineer BIST, test chip, measurement DFT / silicon validation engineer Controller RTL, cocotb or UVM-style verification RTL / design verification engineer (the largest hiring area) A real shuttle tapeout A rare differentiator for a fresh graduate

Many memory design teams are based in India, notably in Bengaluru and Hyderabad.

Honest limits

SRAM on 130 or 180 nm processes runs at roughly 100 to 300 MHz: industry values the methodology and the measurements, not the raw speed. Open DRC and LVS decks are accepted on open shuttles, but industry signoff uses Calibre. Fabrication access (shuttles, prices, providers) changes quickly.

docs.title: 17.3 Can a 4 GB RAM be designed with open-source tools?
docs.text:
A common question from students: could I design a complete 4 GB RAM myself with free tools? It depends on what "a 4 GB RAM" means.

Meaning Open tools? Manufacturable? A 4 GB RAM chip No No: no open DRAM process exists, and SRAM would be far too big A 4 GB module or board using commercial DRAM chips Yes: KiCad Yes: any PCB fab and assembly house A 4 GB memory system (your own controller and DRAM) Yes: LiteDRAM, Verilator, FPGA tools Runs on a real FPGA board

The short answer is: not as a single chip; yes as a module built from commercial DRAM chips; and yes as a memory system with your own controller.

Example 17.1: The area maths of a 4 GB chip

Without a DRAM process, the only memory one could build on an open PDK is SRAM. A quick calculation shows why that cannot reach 4 GB.

  1. 4 GB in bits: \(4 \times 2^{30} \times 8 = 34.4\) billion bits.
  2. SKY130 6T bitcell area: about 2 µm². With about 60 per cent array efficiency, the area per bit including periphery is about \(2/0.6 = 3.3\) µm².
  3. Total silicon area: \(34.4 \times 10^{9} \times 3.3\ \mu\text{m}^2 = 1.14 \times 10^{11}\ \mu\text{m}^2 \approx 114{,}000\ \text{mm}^2\), about 115,000 mm² or 1150 cm².
  4. The reticle limit (the largest single chip a scanner can expose) is about 858 mm² (26 × 33 mm), so \(114{,}000/858 \approx 133\): about 130 or more maximum-size chips.
  5. A 200 mm wafer has an area of \(\pi \times 100^2 = 31{,}400\) mm², so \(114{,}000/31{,}400 = 3.6\): about four full wafers of pure memory, and the yield of a maximum-size die at 130 nm is low without redundancy and repair.
  6. Compare a commercial 1β DRAM: its 1T1C cell is about 0.001 µm², roughly 2000 times smaller per bit than the SKY130 SRAM cell. A full 4 GB fits on a single DRAM die of very roughly 60 to 80 mm² (an estimate) that costs a few dollars to make. Array efficiency, the fraction of die area that is actual memory cells rather than decoders, sense amplifiers and wiring, matters as much as cell size.

How much SRAM does fit on open silicon?

Silicon available Area Approx. SRAM capacity One Tiny Tapeout tile ~0.016 mm² A few hundred bytes A typical shuttle slot ~10 mm² ~300 KB A full reticle-size chip ~858 mm² ~30 MB 4 GB – ~130 times the biggest possible chip

A realistic silicon target is therefore 1 KB to a few hundred KB, which is exactly what industry SRAM test chips look like anyway.

Option 1 (recommended): a 4 GB DDR4 SO-DIMM in KiCad. You can design a complete, working 4 GB module with open tools by using commercial DRAM chips: four 8 Gbit x16 DDR4 chips (from Micron, Samsung or SK hynix) give 4 GB in a single 64-bit rank (\(4 \times 16 = 64\) bits; \(4 \times 8\ \text{Gbit} = 32\ \text{Gbit} = 4\) GB). Add an SPD EEPROM, decoupling capacitors and termination resistors on a 6 to 8 layer impedance-controlled, length-matched PCB. The tools are KiCad for schematic and layout with length tuning and differential pairs; basic signal-integrity simulation with vendor IBIS models in KiCad's ngspice simulator; optionally openEMS for field-solver analysis; SPD contents written to the JEDEC SPD specification and verified with Linux decode-dimms; a functional test in a laptop or mini PC with Memtest86+; and fabrication files (Gerbers, drill, BOM, pick-and-place) for a PCB fab offering impedance control and BGA assembly. Antmicro has published open-source KiCad designs for DDR4 SO-DIMMs and DRAM test boards, which make excellent references. The difficulty is medium to hard, and a prototype costs a few hundred dollars.

Option 2: a memory system with your own controller. Use LiteDRAM as the reference design, simulate with Verilator and cocotb, explore policies with Ramulator 2.0, and run it on an ECP5 FPGA board with the Yosys and nextpnr flow. The controller design is the same for 128 MB or 4 GB: capacity comes from the DRAM chips, not the controller.

Option 3 (stretch): gain-cell eDRAM on an open PDK. A gain-cell eDRAM uses two or three ordinary transistors (2T or 3T) and stores charge on the gate of one of them instead of on a dedicated capacitor. Like DRAM, the charge leaks and must be refreshed, so you can measure retention time on real silicon, an active research topic. A classic 1T1C cell built with the MIM (metal-insulator-metal) capacitors available on these PDKs is impractical, because the capacitors are far too large.

Figure 17.1. Three combined open-source projects: an SRAM test chip (with a gain-cell eDRAM stretch) using Xschem, ngspice, Magic, KLayout, OpenRAM and LibreLane on a shuttle; a 4 GB DDR4 SO-DIMM in KiCad with openEMS and Memtest86+; and a memory controller on an FPGA using Verilator, cocotb, Yosys, nextpnr and Ramulator

Together the three projects cover the chip, the module and the controller.

docs.title: 17.4 Working with a systems partner
docs.text:
A memory design effort needs more than a fab. A systems partner, such as an Indian server maker that does not make chips, fills two other gaps: compute infrastructure for running EDA tools, and a system partner and customer, so that memory designs reach real servers. It cannot supply fabrication, PDKs or foundry bitcells, EDA licences, DRAM dies, or packaging and chip testing. The current products and capabilities of any named company should be confirmed with the company itself, as with every vendor and product named in this part of the book.

Figure 17.2. The memory product value chain: design (EDA on partner compute), fab (TSMC, GF or open PDK), package and test (OSATs), module or board (PCB fab and assembly) and system (servers and AI clusters), with the partner helping at design and system stages

India's ecosystem is growing around the middle stages too: Micron's assembly and test plant at Sanand, Gujarat, and Indian OSAT projects from Tata, Kaynes and CG Semi.

Sizing the compute.

Project CPU cores Big-memory servers Storage GPUs Open-PDK SRAM test chip 64–256 Not needed (256–512 GB fine) 10–50 TB Not needed TSMC N7 SRAM macro / compiler (10–30 engineers) 500–2000 2–4 with 1–2 TB 100–500 TB Optional TSMC N7 LPDDR5X / DDR5 controller and PHY (50–150 engineers) 2000–10,000 5–10 with 2–4 TB 0.5–2 PB Useful Full memory-centric SoC / AI accelerator 10,000+ 10+ with 4 TB Multi-PB Yes

An on-premise, isolated cluster run by a trusted partner can meet the strict security requirements of advanced-node PDKs more easily than a general-purpose cloud account.

Product opportunities.

Product What you design Feasibility CXL memory expander card CXL controller chip (N7 plus licensed PHY) and a card PCB with DDR5 High DDR5 RDIMM / MRDIMM made locally Module PCB, SPD, thermal design (DRAM dies bought in) Very high; the most achievable, no custom chip Memory-rich AI accelerator Large SRAM or compute-in-memory chip (N7) Medium; large effort, high impact SRAM compiler IP Compiler at N7 / GF 22FDX High; an IP business Memory test / validation platform Rowhammer, reliability, error-rate and CXL testing on real servers Very high; low cost, publishable Memory tiering software (DRAM, CXL and SSD) Linux kernel / runtime High; software only HBM / DRAM chips – Not possible; needs a DRAM maker

A phased roadmap: phase 1 (0 to 12 months) builds the team and methodology with an open-PDK SRAM test chip, an FPGA controller and a KiCad DDR4 or DDR5 module; phase 2 (6 to 18 months) delivers a first product with no custom chip, a DDR5 RDIMM qualified on partner servers, and a memory test platform; phase 3 (12 to 30 months) targets advanced-node silicon, a low-Vmin SRAM macro or compiler on a TSMC N7 shuttle; phase 4 (24 to 48 months) builds a system chip, a CXL memory expander controller or an SRAM or compute-in-memory AI accelerator. Still not possible: your own DRAM chip (DDR5, LPDDR6 or HBM DRAM dies) or NAND. The realistic route there is partnership with a DRAM maker, since HBM base dies are increasingly co-designed with customers. Programmes such as the India Semiconductor Mission and its Design Linked Incentive (DLI) scheme and the C2S programme support design and tapeout funding.

docs.text:
The exercises of this book can all be done with free, open-source tools; the industry uses commercial equivalents, and knowing both helps when applying for jobs. The toolbox is:

C1 out 0 1p
