Three paths into the memory industry. Memory circuit design: SRAM cells, sense amplifiers and timing (Exercises 2.5, 2.6 and 15.6); employers are memory-compiler teams, CPU and GPU companies and DRAM makers' design centres. Board and signal integrity: module and motherboard design, high-speed signals and power (Exercises 12.4, 12.5, 13.5, 14.4 and 14.5); employers are module makers, server and PC companies. Controllers and verification: memory controllers in Verilog, testbenches and FPGA prototypes (Exercise 3.5); the largest hiring area in chip design.

docs.title: 17.6 Summary
docs.text:
• DRAM is a market of about USD 130 billion or more; DDR is about 40 per cent of revenue, LPDDR 25 to 30, HBM 20 to 30 and rising; SK hynix, Samsung and Micron lead, with CXMT rising.
  • The best open-source route to real RAM silicon is an SRAM macro test chip on an open PDK plus an FPGA controller; DRAM and the LPDDR6 PHY cannot be built with open processes.
  • A 4 GB SRAM chip would need about 115,000 mm², about 130 maximum-size chips; a 4 GB module (four 8 Gbit x16 DDR4 chips) can be designed in KiCad, and a memory system with your own controller can run on an FPGA.
  • A systems partner can supply compute and a path to market, not chips; the most achievable product is a locally made DDR5 module.
  • Three career paths: memory circuit design, board and signal integrity, controllers and verification.

docs.title: 17.7 Exercises
docs.text:
Exercise 17.1. How much SRAM fits into a 10 mm² shuttle slot at 3.3 µm² per bit, and how many bytes is that? Compare with the table in Section 17.3.

Answer

\(10\ \text{mm}^2 = 10^{7}\ \mu\text{m}^2\), and \(10^7/3.3 = 3.03 \times 10^{6}\) bits \(= 379\) KB. The table gives "about 300 KB", which allows for the pad ring and test circuits that take part of the area.

Exercise 17.2. Four 8 Gbit x16 DDR4 chips make a 4 GB module. How many chips would you need for an 8 GB single-rank module, and which chip organisation gives a 64-bit rank?

Answer

With 8 Gbit x16 chips, four chips give 64 bits and \(4 \times 1\ \text{GB} = 4\) GB. For 8 GB in one rank, use 16 Gbit x16 chips (four chips again), or eight 8 Gbit x8 chips for 8 GB (eight x8 chips give 64 bits, \(8 \times 1\ \text{GB} = 8\) GB).

Exercise 17.3. Run the RC netlist of Section 17.5 (R = 1 kΩ, C = 1 pF, a pulse from 0 V to 1 V lasting 5 ns). What is the time constant, and how close does the output come to 1 V within the 5 ns pulse?

Answer

\(\tau = RC = 1\ \text{k}\Omega \times 1\ \text{pF} = 1\) ns. After 5 ns the output has reached \(1 - e^{-5} = 0.993\) of the final value, about 0.993 V. After one time constant it reached 63 per cent.

Exercise 17.4. The module project of Chapters 11 to 14 uses KiCad, ngspice, Python, pytest and an automatic router. To which of the three career paths does each skill contribute: (a) writing the SPD checksum code; (b) simulating the termination study; (c) simulating a sense amplifier; (d) writing a cocotb timing checker?

Answer

(a) Board and signal integrity (module firmware and test data). (b) Board and signal integrity. (c) Memory circuit design. (d) Controllers and verification.

Exercise 17.5 (Assignment 14: capstone, pick one). Do real engineering on an open problem. Options: (a) solve the module's DRAM via fan-out (Section 14.2) as an integer program with scipy.optimize.milp; (b) plan a 1 KB SRAM test chip with a built-in self-test (March C−) and a measurement plan for Vmin and access time; (c) design a 4 GB DDR4 SO-DIMM in KiCad from an open reference design. Deliver code or design files plus a two-page report.

Answer

Success criteria: (a) every ball gets a via site and the tests pass; (b) the plan names every block and test; (c) design-rule check reports 0 violations, with a length-matching report. For (b), the March C− test is the sequence: up the addresses write 0; up: read 0, write 1; up: read 1, write 0; down: read 0, write 1; down: read 1, write 0; down: read 0. Scope it so you can finish it: a small finished project beats a big unfinished one.

docs.title: Chapter 4: The SRAM Family
docs.text: SRAM is the fastest memory that exists, and it needs no refresh. It is built from ordinary logic transistors, so it can sit on the same chip as the processor. Its weakness is size: each bit needs several transistors, so SRAM costs far more silicon area per bit than DRAM. This chapter surveys the variants of SRAM, from the six-transistor cell inside every cache to the content-addressable memories in network routers, and shows how each trades speed, density, power and interface simplicity. For each one it states how it works, its strengths and weaknesses, and where it is used.

docs.title: 4.1 6T SRAM
docs.text:
The six-transistor cell of Section 2.2 is the workhorse. Two cross-coupled inverters form a latch and two access transistors connect it to a bitline pair. To read, both bitlines are precharged high, the wordline is raised and a sense amplifier detects which bitline starts to fall. To write, strong drivers force the bitlines to opposite values and overpower the latch.

Strengths. Very fast, well under a nanosecond for small first-level cache arrays; no refresh; made in the same process as the logic.

Weaknesses. Six transistors per bit make it many times larger than a DRAM cell, and SRAM cell area has shrunk only slowly at the newest process nodes (Section 15.6). Idle cells still leak current. Reading must not flip the cell and writing must flip it, and these goals conflict as supply voltage drops.

Where it is used. Registers and register files, the L1, L2 and L3 caches of processors and graphics chips, GPU shared memory, on-chip buffers in AI accelerators and network chips, and stacked cache dies such as AMD's 3D V-Cache.

docs.title: 4.2 8T and 10T SRAM
docs.text:
An 8T cell adds a two-transistor read port to the 6T cell. A separate read wordline and read bitline sense the stored value through a buffer transistor, so a read never disturbs the latch. 10T designs add further transistors, for example for a differential read port or to allow reliable operation near the transistor threshold voltage.

Strengths. Read stability and write ability are designed separately, so the cell works at much lower supply voltages. The separate ports allow one read and one write in the same cycle, which suits register files.

Weaknesses. The cell is noticeably larger than 6T and needs extra wiring per cell, and the peripheral circuits are more complex.

Where it is used. Register files in processors and graphics chips, multi-ported buffers, and ultra-low-power chips for wearables and the Internet of Things that run at very low voltage to save energy.

docs.title: 4.3 Asynchronous SRAM
docs.text:
This is a standalone SRAM chip with no clock. The system places an address on the pins, asserts chip-enable together with output-enable (to read) or write-enable (to write), and the data is valid after a fixed access time: typically tens of nanoseconds for standard parts and around 10 ns for fast ones.

Strengths. Extremely simple to connect to a microcontroller, FPGA or older processor; predictable timing; low-power versions can retain data on a small battery for years.

Weaknesses. Slow and low in bandwidth by modern standards; small capacities (kilobits to tens of megabits); expensive per bit compared with DRAM.

Where it is used. Older embedded systems, industrial controllers, battery-backed configuration storage, retro computers and FPGA prototyping boards.

docs.title: 4.4 Synchronous SRAM
docs.text:
In a synchronous SRAM, inputs and outputs are registered on a clock edge. Pipelined versions add an output register for a higher clock speed; flow-through versions give data one cycle sooner. Burst modes read consecutive addresses automatically, and "zero bus turnaround" variants remove idle cycles when switching between reads and writes.

Strengths. Much higher throughput than asynchronous SRAM, and timing that is easy to fit into a clocked design.

Weaknesses. More pins and power; a shrinking niche because large on-chip SRAM has replaced most external caches.

Where it is used. Networking line cards, lookup tables in telecom and test equipment, and the external second-level caches ("pipeline burst cache") on PC motherboards of the 1990s.

docs.title: 4.5 QDR SRAM
docs.text:
Quad data rate SRAM has separate read and write data ports, and each port transfers data on both clock edges. Two words in plus two words out give four transfers per clock cycle. Because reads and writes never share a bus, there is no turnaround penalty, and fully random accesses run at full speed.

Strengths. A very high random-access rate with low, fixed latency, ideal when every access goes to a different address.

Weaknesses. Expensive, power-hungry, small in capacity and with many pins.

Where it is used. Packet lookup tables, flow statistics counters and queue pointers in routers and switches, and radar and other signal-processing equipment.

docs.title: 4.6 PSRAM (pseudo-static RAM)
docs.text:
Inside, PSRAM uses DRAM 1T1C cells, but a built-in controller refreshes them automatically, so the outside world sees a simple SRAM-like interface with no refresh commands. Modern parts often use a serial interface (quad SPI or 8-bit octal) with very few pins.

Strengths. Much denser and cheaper than SRAM, typically a few megabytes in a tiny package, with a very simple interface.

Weaknesses. Slower than true SRAM; an access that collides with an internal refresh can take longer; standby current is higher than that of SRAM.

Where it is used. Microcontroller boards such as ESP32 modules with a few MB of PSRAM, IoT devices that drive displays or buffer audio, and older mobile phones, where it was sold as "cellular RAM".

docs.title: 4.7 1T-SRAM
docs.text:
Developed by MoSys, 1T-SRAM uses a one-transistor DRAM cell but hides refresh and row management behind an SRAM-style interface, using many small banks so that refresh rarely gets in the way of an access.

Strengths. Several times denser than 6T SRAM while keeping SRAM-like, predictable latency.

Weaknesses. It needs licensed technology and process support and is largely a historical design today.

Where it is used. The Nintendo GameCube (main memory plus embedded memory in its graphics chip) and the Nintendo Wii.

docs.title: 4.8 TCAM (ternary content-addressable memory)
docs.text:
Normal RAM takes an address and returns data. A content-addressable memory works the other way round: you present a search key, every stored entry compares itself with the key in parallel, and the memory returns the address of the first match in a single operation. "Ternary" means each stored bit can be 0, 1 or X ("don't care"), so one entry can match a whole range, such as an IP prefix like 192.168.x.x. Each cell needs storage for the value and the mask, plus comparison logic.

Strengths. Constant-time lookup no matter how large the table is; ideal for longest-prefix matching and rule tables.

Weaknesses. Very high power (every entry is compared on every search), large area and high cost.

Where it is used. Routers and switches for IP route lookup, access-control lists and quality-of-service rules. Simpler binary CAMs also appear inside processors, for example in the translation lookaside buffers (TLBs) that translate virtual to physical addresses.

Example 4.1: A tiny TCAM lookup

A router table holds three entries, kept in order from the most specific to the least specific. A bit shown as X matches either value. For clarity the keys are written as dotted decimal, where x means all eight bits are X.

Entry Stored pattern Meaning Output port 1 10.1.2.x one subnet A 2 10.1.x.x a larger block B 3 x.x.x.x everything else C

Search for 10.1.2.7. All three entries compare at the same instant, and entries 1, 2 and 3 all match. The memory returns the first (highest-priority) match, entry 1, so the packet goes to port A. A search for 10.1.9.4 matches entries 2 and 3 only and returns B; 172.16.0.1 matches only entry 3 and returns C. Because the entries are ordered from longest prefix to shortest, "first match" is the same as "longest prefix match", which is what routers need.

docs.title: 4.9 SRAM family summary
docs.text: Type How it works Where it is used 6T SRAM 6 transistors per bit, no refresh needed CPU and GPU caches, registers, on-chip buffers 8T/10T SRAM Extra transistors for a separate read port and low-voltage stability Low-power chips, register files Asynchronous SRAM No clock, simple interface Older embedded systems Synchronous SRAM Clocked interface Networking, legacy caches QDR SRAM Separate read and write ports, 4 transfers per clock Network packet lookup PSRAM DRAM cell with built-in refresh and an SRAM-style interface Microcontrollers (ESP32), IoT, older phones 1T-SRAM DRAM cell behind an SRAM interface Nintendo GameCube and Wii TCAM Searches all entries at once by content Routers and switches (IP route lookup)

docs.title: 4.10 Summary
docs.text:
• SRAM is the fastest memory and needs no refresh, but costs the most area per bit.
  • Variants differ in cell (6T, 8T, 10T), interface (asynchronous, synchronous, QDR) and cell type behind the interface (PSRAM and 1T-SRAM hide DRAM cells).
  • 8T cells protect the latch from reads with a separate read port, and so work at lower voltage.
  • QDR separates read and write buses to give four transfers per clock without turnaround.
  • A TCAM compares all entries in parallel and supports "don't care" bits, giving constant-time longest-prefix lookup at a high power cost.

docs.title: 4.11 Exercises
docs.text:
Exercise 4.1. Why can PSRAM look like SRAM from outside although it is built from DRAM cells? What does it give up compared with true SRAM?

Answer

A built-in controller refreshes the 1T1C cells on its own, so the system never sends refresh commands and sees an SRAM-style interface. In return PSRAM is slower than true SRAM, an access that collides with an internal refresh can take longer, and standby current is higher. What it gains is density and cost: a few megabytes in a tiny, cheap package.

Exercise 4.2. Explain in two sentences why an 8T cell can work at a lower supply voltage than a 6T cell.

Answer

In a 6T cell the same access transistors are used for reading and writing, so read stability and write ability pull against each other as the voltage falls. An 8T cell reads through a separate two-transistor read port that never disturbs the latch, so the two goals can be designed separately.

Exercise 4.3. Choose the best SRAM type for each need: (a) a processor's first-level cache; (b) a router's per-packet lookup table where every access goes to a different address; (c) matching an IP address against a list of prefixes in one operation; (d) a microcontroller needing a few megabytes at low cost with few pins.

Answer

(a) 6T SRAM on the processor die. (b) QDR SRAM, with separate read and write ports and no turnaround penalty. (c) TCAM. (d) PSRAM with a quad or octal SPI interface.

Exercise 4.4. Using Example 4.1's table, which port does the address 10.2.0.1 go to, and why?

Answer

Entry 1 (10.1.2.x) needs the second number to be 1, so it does not match. Entry 2 (10.1.x.x) also needs the second number to be 1, so it does not match. Entry 3 matches everything, so the packet goes to port C.

Exercise 4.5. A QDR SRAM has two data ports, each 18 bits wide, on a clock of 400 MHz (a supposed figure for this exercise). Each port transfers on both clock edges. Find the data rate of one port and the total transfers per clock cycle.

Answer

One port makes 2 transfers per clock, so \(2 \times 400 = 800\) MT/s, and with 18 bits \(800 \times 18 / 8 = 1800\) MB/s \(= 1.8\) GB/s. Two ports (one read, one write) make \(2 + 2 = 4\) transfers per clock cycle, hence "quad" data rate; read and write together reach 3.6 GB/s, with no turnaround penalty because they never share a bus.

docs.title: Chapter 1: What RAM Is and Why There Are Several Kinds
docs.text: This chapter lays the groundwork for everything that follows. It explains what random-access memory does, how a bit and a byte relate to the capacity figures on a box, why computers stack several kinds of memory into a hierarchy, and how the family of RAM technologies is organised. It then defines the vocabulary of speed: clock frequency, megatransfers per second, bus width, bandwidth and latency, with the two formulas that every memory engineer uses daily. Later chapters use these terms without further comment, so it is worth working the examples here with a pencil.

docs.title: 1.1 What RAM is
docs.text:
Random-access memory is memory in which any location can be read or written in about the same time, no matter which location was used last. The processor gives the memory an address, a number that names a location, and the memory returns or stores the data held there. This is different from a tape or a spinning disk, where reaching data that is far from the current position takes much longer. In a computer, RAM holds the programs and the data the processor is working on right now, while slower storage (an SSD or a disk) holds everything else.

A kitchen is a useful picture. The processor is the chef, the SSD or hard disk is the pantry, huge but far away, and RAM is the counter next to the stove: smaller, but everything on it can be reached at once. Before cooking, ingredients are brought from the pantry to the counter. In the same way every program and file that is opened is copied from storage into RAM first. More RAM means more things can be open at once without the machine slowing down, in the way that a bigger counter lets the chef work on several dishes together.

Almost all RAM is built from millions or billions of tiny storage cells, each holding one bit. The cells are arranged in a grid of rows and columns. A horizontal wire called the wordline (WL) selects a row, and vertical wires called bitlines (BL) carry data in and out of the cells of that row. Small amplifiers at the edge of the array, the sense amplifiers, detect the very small signals on the bitlines and turn them into clean 0s and 1s. The next two chapters look inside these cells and this grid in detail.

Typical amounts are a few gigabytes to a few tens of gigabytes in a laptop or desktop and one to four terabytes in a large server.

docs.title: 1.2 Bits, bytes and capacity
docs.text:
A bit holds one of two states, 0 or 1, like a light switch that is off or on. Eight bits make a byte, which has \(2^8 = 256\) possible patterns, enough for one letter of text. Every photograph, song and program is a very long row of such switches.

The size of the numbers involved is easy to underestimate. A memory module that stores 32 GB of data holds \(32 \times 2^{30} \times 8 = 2^{38}\) bits, which is about 275 billion switches. Each one is a tiny electric charge that must be read and rewritten correctly, millions of times per second.

Example 1.1: How many cells in 32 GB?

  1. 1 GB of DRAM is \(2^{30}\) bytes, so 32 GB is \(32 \times 2^{30} = 2^{5} \times 2^{30} = 2^{35}\) bytes.
  2. Each byte is 8 bits \(= 2^3\), so the total is \(2^{35} \times 2^{3} = 2^{38}\) bits.
  3. \(2^{38} = 274{,}877{,}906{,}944\), about \(2.75 \times 10^{11}\), or roughly 275 billion bit cells.

Two unit conventions are used throughout the book. Capacity of memory is binary: a "gigabyte" of DRAM is \(2^{30}\) bytes, and chip sizes in gigabits (Gb) are binary multiples too. Bandwidth is decimal: 1 GB/s is 1000 MB/s. Mixing the two is a common source of small arithmetic errors, so units are always stated.

docs.title: 1.3 The memory hierarchy
docs.text:
No single memory is fast, large, cheap and low-power at once, so computers combine several. Small, very fast memories sit close to the processor and hold the data used most often; each level farther away is larger and cheaper per bit but slower. Hardware and software move data between the levels automatically, so most accesses are served by the fast levels. Figure 1.1 shows the levels as they stood in 2026; the numbers are typical orders of magnitude, not exact values for any particular machine.

Figure 1.1. The memory hierarchy as a pyramid: registers, SRAM caches, HBM or DRAM main memory, CXL far memory, SSD storage, with typical latency and capacity at each level

Registers and caches are SRAM, built inside the processor. Main memory is DRAM, the main subject of this book. A newer tier, CXL memory, sits between local DRAM and storage; it is DRAM reached over PCIe-style wires and is described in Chapter 8.

The gaps between levels are so wide that a logarithmic scale is needed to draw them. Figure 1.2 repeats the typical times and adds a second reading: if one processor step took one second, how long would each fetch take?

Figure 1.2. A log-scale bar chart of the time to fetch one piece of data: CPU register 0.3 ns, L1 1 ns, L3 10 ns, DRAM 80 ns, NVMe SSD 80 microseconds, hard disk 8 ms, each with its value scaled to a one-second processor step

The scaled figures make the point vividly. If a register access takes about one second, a DRAM access takes more than four minutes, an SSD more than three days and a hard disk about ten months. A processor that had to wait for storage on every access would spend nearly all its time idle. DRAM is roughly a thousand times faster than an SSD (80 ns against 80 µs), and that is why the working set of a program is kept in RAM.

docs.title: 1.4 Volatile and non-volatile memory
docs.text: Volatile memory loses its contents when power is removed. SRAM and DRAM, the two technologies behind almost all working memory, are volatile. Non-volatile memory keeps its data with the power off. Flash memory, used in SSDs and USB sticks, is non-volatile but is not true RAM: it is written in large pages, erased in even larger blocks and wears out after a limited number of writes. A family of emerging non-volatile RAMs (MRAM, FeRAM, ReRAM, phase-change memory) tries to combine RAM-like byte access with non-volatility; Chapter 9 describes them.

docs.title: 1.5 The RAM family tree
docs.text:
Figure 1.3 groups every memory covered in this book. The volatile branch splits into SRAM (on-chip memories and small standalone parts) and DRAM, which itself branches into families tuned for different goals: capacity and cost (DDR), power (LPDDR), per-pin speed (GDDR) and raw bandwidth (HBM). The non-volatile branch holds the emerging memories plus NVDIMMs, which combine DRAM with flash.

Figure 1.3. A tree with RAM at the top, splitting into volatile (SRAM and DRAM branches) and non-volatile (MRAM, FeRAM, ReRAM, PCM, NVDIMM)

A quick table fixes the personalities of the main families before the later chapters study each one in turn.

Type Personality Where you find it Speed today (approx.) DDR5 The all-rounder: big capacity, plug-in modules Desktops, servers 4800 to 8800 MT/s per pin LPDDR5X The energy saver: low voltage, soldered next to the processor Phones, thin laptops, Apple Silicon Macs 8533 to 10,700 MT/s per pin GDDR7 The sprinter: very fast pins, runs hot Graphics cards 28 to 32 Gbps per pin HBM3E The skyscraper: 8 to 12 dies stacked, 1024 wires wide AI accelerators about 1.2 TB/s per stack SRAM The pocket notebook: tiny, fastest, no refresh Caches inside every processor about 1 ns access

docs.title: 1.6 Speed terms: MHz, MT/s, Gbps and bandwidth
docs.text:
Memory speeds are quoted in several units that are easy to confuse.

  • Clock frequency (MHz) is how many clock cycles occur per second. Modern memory moves data on both the rising and the falling clock edge, so the clock number is half the data rate. Marketing labels such as "DDR5-6400" give the data rate, not the clock.
  • MT/s (megatransfers per second) counts how many times per second each data pin carries a new symbol. DDR5-6400 runs at 6400 MT/s on a 3200 MHz clock.
  • Gbps per pin is the same idea in larger units, used for very fast interfaces. 32 Gbps per pin for GDDR7 means 32,000 MT/s. With multi-level signalling a transfer can carry more than one bit (Section 3.4).
  • Bus width is how many data pins move in parallel: 64 bits for a standard DDR DIMM, 16 bits per LPDDR5 channel, 32 bits per GDDR chip, 1024 or 2048 bits per HBM stack.
  • Bandwidth is the total data moved per second: data rate multiplied by bus width.
\[\text{Bandwidth (GB/s)} = \frac{\text{data rate (MT/s)} \times \text{bus width (bits)}}{8 \times 1000}\]

Example 1.2: Peak bandwidth of one DDR5-6400 DIMM

  1. Data rate 6400 MT/s on a 64-bit bus: \(6400 \times 64 = 409{,}600\) megabits per second.
  2. Divide by 8 bits per byte: \(409{,}600 / 8 = 51{,}200\) MB/s.
  3. Divide by 1000 to get GB/s: 51.2 GB/s.
  4. A desktop with two such channels has a peak of \(2 \times 51.2 = 102.4\) GB/s.
  5. Real programs typically reach 70 to 90 per cent of the peak, because of refresh, bank conflicts and switching between reads and writes. For the dual-channel desktop that is about 72 to 92 GB/s.

For per-pin rates in Gbps the answer comes out directly in GB/s when multiplied by the width and divided by 8, which is how GDDR and HBM figures are usually worked.

docs.title: 1.7 Latency: CAS latency and nanoseconds
docs.text:
Latency is the delay between asking for data and receiving it. The most quoted number is CAS latency (CL): the number of clock cycles between a column read command and the first data appearing. Because the clock gets faster with each generation, CL has to be converted to nanoseconds before parts can be compared. The clock in MHz is half the data rate in MT/s, and one clock cycle lasts \(1000 / \text{MHz}\) nanoseconds, so a cycle lasts \(2000 / \text{data rate}\) nanoseconds. Hence

\[\text{CAS latency (ns)} = \frac{\text{CL} \times 2000}{\text{data rate (MT/s)}}\]

Example 1.3: The same ten nanoseconds twice

  • DDR4-3200 CL16: \(16 \times 2000 / 3200 = 10\) ns.
  • DDR5-6000 CL30: \(30 \times 2000 / 6000 = 10\) ns.
  • DDR5-4800 CL40: \(40 \times 2000 / 4800 \approx 16.7\) ns.

The first two answers are identical. The DRAM array has barely become faster in twenty years, so the extra speed of each generation goes into bandwidth and not into latency. The full time for a random access from a processor (cache miss, controller queueing, opening a row, CAS and the trip back) is typically 60 to 120 ns, much more than the CAS figure alone.

Do not compare CL numbers across generations

A DDR5 module with CL40 is not slower than a DDR4 module with CL16 in the sense the numbers suggest. Always convert to nanoseconds first.

docs.title: 1.8 Summary
docs.text:
• RAM gives any location about the same access time; it holds what the processor is working on, while storage holds the rest.
  • A bit is one of two states; a byte is eight bits; 32 GB of DRAM holds about 275 billion cells.
  • The memory hierarchy exists because speed, size and cost pull in opposite directions. DRAM is about a thousand times faster than an SSD; caches are built from SRAM.
  • RAM divides into volatile (SRAM, DRAM) and non-volatile families; flash is not true RAM.
  • Bandwidth is data rate times bus width divided by 8 (decimal units); peak figures are never fully reached.
  • CAS latency must be converted to nanoseconds: \(\text{CL} \times 2000 / \text{MT/s}\).

docs.title: 1.9 Exercises
docs.text:
Exercise 1.1. A laptop has 16 GB of DRAM. How many bit cells is that, in powers of two and approximately in decimal?

Answer

\(16 \times 2^{30} \times 8 = 2^{4} \times 2^{30} \times 2^{3} = 2^{37}\) bits \(= 137{,}438{,}953{,}472\), about \(1.37 \times 10^{11}\) or 137 billion cells.

Exercise 1.2. Compute the peak bandwidth of a single 64-bit DDR5-4800 DIMM and of a dual-channel DDR5-6400 desktop. By what factor is the second larger?

Answer

DDR5-4800: \(4800 \times 64 / 8 / 1000 = 38.4\) GB/s. Dual-channel DDR5-6400: \(2 \times 51.2 = 102.4\) GB/s. The ratio is \(102.4 / 38.4 \approx 2.67\).

Exercise 1.3. Convert to nanoseconds and rank the three modules: DDR4-2400 CL17, DDR5-5600 CL36, DDR5-6400 CL32.

Answer

DDR4-2400 CL17: \(17 \times 2000 / 2400 = 14.17\) ns. DDR5-5600 CL36: \(36 \times 2000 / 5600 = 12.86\) ns. DDR5-6400 CL32: \(32 \times 2000 / 6400 = 10.0\) ns. From lowest latency to highest: DDR5-6400 CL32, DDR5-5600 CL36, DDR4-2400 CL17.

Exercise 1.4. DRAM takes about 80 ns to fetch a value and an NVMe SSD about 80 µs. If one processor step took one second, how long would each fetch take? Use 0.3 ns for the step.

Answer

The scale factor is \(1\,\text{s} / 0.3\,\text{ns} = 3.33 \times 10^{9}\). DRAM: \(80 \times 10^{-9} \times 3.33 \times 10^{9} = 267\) s, about 4.4 minutes. SSD: \(80 \times 10^{-6} \times 3.33 \times 10^{9} = 267{,}000\) s, about 3.1 days. The ratio is 1000.

Exercise 1.5 (Assignment 1: a bandwidth and capacity calculator). Write a small Python script with two functions, bandwidth(mts, width_bits) returning GB/s and capacity(chips, gbit_per_chip, ecc_chips) returning the data capacity and the raw capacity in GB. Use them to print a table for DDR5-4800 and DDR5-6400 on a 64-bit bus and for a module of 20 chips of 16 Gb of which 4 are ECC chips.

Answer 

def bandwidth(mts, width_bits):
    """Peak bandwidth in GB/s (decimal)."""
    return mts * width_bits / 8 / 1000

def capacity(chips, gbit_per_chip, ecc_chips):
    """Return (data GB, raw GB); 1 GB = 8 Gb."""
    raw = chips * gbit_per_chip / 8
    data = (chips - ecc_chips) * gbit_per_chip / 8
    return data, raw

for rate in (4800, 6400):
    print(f"DDR5-{rate}, 64-bit: {bandwidth(rate, 64):.1f} GB/s")
print("module:", capacity(20, 16, 4))
Expected output: DDR5-4800 gives 38.4 GB/s, DDR5-6400 gives 51.2 GB/s, and the module gives 32.0 GB of data from 40.0 GB raw. Hint: divide bits by 8 for bytes and by 1000 to go from MB/s to GB/s.
